On Boxing Day the whole family gathered together again at dinner at my father’s. There were no strangers except the Right Honourable “To-be-sure” and Dr. Bresser. As we were sitting at table in the familiar dining-room I could not help having a lively remembrance of that evening when we two first plainly recognised our love. Dr. Bresser had the same thought.
“Have you forgotten the game of piquet which I was playing with your father, while you chatted over the fire with Baron Tilling?” he asked me. “I seemed, it is true, quite absorbed in my play, but nevertheless I had my ear cocked in your direction, and heard from the sound of the voices﻿—for I could not catch the words﻿—something which awoke in me the conviction, ‘Those two will come together.’ And now that I observe you together a new conviction arises in me, ‘Those two are and will remain happy together.’ ”
“I admire your penetration, doctor. Yes, we *are* happy. Shall we remain so? That, unfortunately, depends not on ourselves but on Fate.﻿ ﻿… Over every happiness there hangs a danger, and the more heartfelt is the former so much the more terrible the latter.”
“What have *you* to fear?”
“Death.”
“Ah, yes! That did not occur to me. As a physician, it is true, I have frequent opportunities of meeting the gentleman, but I do not think of him. And, indeed, for young and healthy people, like the happy pair we are speaking of, he lies so far in the distance﻿—”
“What is a soldier better for youth and health?”
“Chase away such ideas, dear baroness. There is really no war in prospect. Is it not true, your excellency,” he said, turning to the Minister, “that at present the dark point so often spoken of is not visible?”
“ ‘Point’ is far too little to say,” he replied. “It is rather a black, heavy cloud.”
I trembled to my heart’s core.
“What,” I cried out sharply, “what do you mean?”
“Denmark is going altogether too far﻿—”
“Oh, Denmark?” I said, much relieved. “Then the cloud is not threatening us?

节礼日那天，全家人又聚在父亲家中用餐。席上除了那位「诚然」大人 和布雷瑟医生之外，没有外客。当我们在这间熟悉的餐厅里落座时，我不由得生动地忆起我们两人头一回明确认出彼此爱情的那一晚。布雷瑟医生也想起了同一件事。
「你忘了我和你父亲打皮克牌、你却和蒂林男爵在炉边谈心的那一晚吗？」他问我，「我表面上确实全神贯注在牌上，可我毕竟竖着一只耳朵朝你们那边，从声音里——因为话我是听不清的——听出了某种东西，它在我心里唤醒了一个信念：『这两个人会走到一起。』如今我观察你们俩，心里又生出一个新的信念：『这两个人现在是、而且将始终是幸福的。』」
「我真佩服您的洞察力，医生。是的，我们*是*幸福的。会始终如此吗？可惜，这不取决于我们自己，而取决于命运。……每一份幸福头上都悬着一份危险，前者越深挚，后者便越可怕。」
「*你*有什么可怕的？」
「死亡。」
「啊，是啊！这我倒没想到。作为医生，我确实常有机会见到那位先生，可我并不去想他。而且，对像我们谈论的这对幸福人儿这样年轻健康的人来说，他还远在天边——」
「对青春和健康，一个军人又有什么用？」

「『点』字说得太轻了，」他答道，「那与其说是一团又黑又沉的云。」

And, as I said, if we fight with the Danes we have nothing to lose in the war, and may improve our power and position in the German Bund. This danger in the one scale﻿—and in the other﻿—? Austria’s consideration in the German Bund, the liberation of Schleswig-Holstein, “fresh laurels in the army’s crown of glory”﻿—i.e., a lot of phrases for school themes and army proclamations﻿—and even that only dubious, for defeat is always just as possible as victory. “But tell me,” I said aloud, turning to the Minister, “are affairs really in so bad a condition? You ministers and diplomatists, have you no means of hindering this conflict? Do you know of no way of preventing it from breaking out?”
“Do you think then, baroness, that it is our office to maintain perpetual peace? That would, to be sure, be a grand mission, only not practicable. We exist only to watch over the interests of our respective states and dynasties, to work against anything that may threaten the diminution of their power, and strive to conquer for them every supremacy possible, jealously to guard the honour of the country, to avenge any insult cast on it﻿—”
“In short,” I interrupted, “to act on the principle of war﻿—to do the enemy, i.e., every other state, all the harm possible, and if a dispute begins, to persist as long as possible in asserting that you are in the right, even if you see you are in the wrong. Eh?”
“To be sure.”
“Till the patience of the two disputants gives way, and they have to begin hacking away at each other. It is horrible.”
“But that is the only way out. How else can a dispute between nations be decided?”
“How then are trials between civilised individuals decided?”
“By the tribunals. But nations have no such over them.”

“I should not do so.”

I guide myself by the rules of honour; but I by no means imply thereby that those rules, as they now exist amongst us, correspond to my own moral ideal. By degrees, as this ideal gains the sovereignty, the conception of honour will also experience a change. Some day an insult one may have experienced, and which is unprovoked, will redound as a disgrace, not on the receiver, but on the savage inflicter; and when this is the case, self-revenge in matters of honour also will fall as much out of use as in civilised society it has become practically out of the question to right oneself in other matters. We stayed a fortnight longer in Vienna. But it was by no means a pleasant holiday to me. This fatal “prospect of war,” which now filled all newspapers and all conversations, robbed me of all pleasure in my life. As often as I thought of any of the things of which my happiness was made up, and especially my possession of a husband who was becoming daily dearer to me, so often was I reminded also of the uncertainty, of the imminent danger which hung over all my happiness, in view of the war which was looming in sight. And so I could not, as the saying is, “feel myself comfortable.” Of the accidents of sickness and death, conflagrations, inundations, in short, all the menaces of Nature and the elements, there are sufficient; but one has habituated oneself not to think about them, and one lives in a certain sense of security in spite of these dangers. But how is it that men have created for themselves other dangers arbitrarily devised by themselves, and thus of their own will and in pure wantonness thrown into artificial eruption the volcanic soil on which the happiness of this life is founded? It is true that people have also accustomed themselves to think of war too as a natural phenomenon, and to speak of it as eluding calculation in the same category with the earthquake or drought﻿—and therefore to think of it as little as possible.

我们在维也纳又待了两个星期。可这对我绝算不上一个愉快的假期。这要命的「战争前景」，如今塞满了所有报纸和所有谈话，夺走了我生活中的一切乐趣。每当我想到构成我幸福的任何一样东西，尤其是想到我拥有一个一天比一天更亲爱的丈夫，我就同时被提醒那无常、那悬在我全部幸福之上的迫近的危险，因为战争已隐隐在望。因而我无法——套句俗话说——「觉得安生」。疾病与死亡的事故、火灾、水灾，总之大自然和自然力的一切威胁，已经够多了；可人们已经习惯于不去想它们，尽管有这些危险，仍活在某种安全感里。然而，人怎么竟又凭空为自己造出另一些由自己任意设计的危险，就这样出于自己的意志、纯粹出于恣意妄为，把今生幸福所依托的火山土壤人为地捅得喷发起来？不错，人们也习惯了把战争同样看作一种自然现象，把它同地震、旱灾归为一类，说它无从逆料——因此也就尽量不去想它。

The principle of nationality was no doubt a thing that with elemental force demanded its field of action, and therefore from this point of view the thing *must* be. By sticking to this idea the painful indignation of my soul subsided a little. “Even the possibility is terrible to me. If it were a certainty, Frederick, I should not be crying so softly and quietly on your shoulder. I should have to shriek and wail out loud. But the possibility, nay, the probability, that in the year which is opening you may be torn from my arms by a marching order. That is quite enough to transport me with anxiety and grief.”
“Bethink you, Martha. You are yourself going to meet a peril, as this Christmas box of yours so charmingly informed me, and yet we two do not think of the cruel possibility which threatens every woman in childbed about as much as every man on the battlefield. Let us enjoy our life, and not think of the death which is impending over the heads of all of us.”
“You are talking just like Aunt Mary, dearest, as if our lot depended on ‘Providence,’ and not on the thoughtlessness, cruelty, excesses, and follies of our fellow-men. Wherein lies the inevitable necessity of this war with Denmark?”
“It has not yet broken out, and there may still﻿—”
“I know, I know; accidents may still happen to avert the evil. But it is not accident, not political intrigues and humours which ought to decide such questions of destiny; but the firm, righteous *will* of mankind. But what is the good of my ‘ought’ or ‘ought not’? I cannot alter the order of things. I can only complain of it. But do help me so far, Frederick!

===Chinese===

「因为我对于一场战役，除了盼它永不发生，不可能有别的愿望。」
回到旅馆、进了卧室之后，我扑到腓特烈的颈上。
「我的人儿！腓特烈！腓特烈！」
「你怎么了，玛尔塔？你哭了；而且今天——大年初一的夜里！为什么流着泪迎接新年？你不幸福吗？我有什么地方得罪了你？」
「你？哦不！不！你给我的幸福只嫌太多——太多了——这反倒叫我不安——」
「迷信了不是，玛尔塔？你这是给自己招来嫉妒的神明，人太幸福时他们就要毁掉它？」
「不是神明；是那些给自己召来灾祸的、丧失理智的人。」
「你是影射这场可能的战争。可它根本还没有定论呢。何必这样提早悲伤？谁知道会不会真打起来？就算打起来，谁知道会不会轮到我开拔？到这儿来，亲爱的，坐下，」他把我拉到沙发上他身边。「别为区区一个可能性浪费眼泪。」
「连这可能性对我也已经可怕极了。倘若成了定局，腓特烈，我就不会这样轻轻地、静静地靠在你肩上哭了。我就只好放声嘶喊哀号了。可是这可能性——不，这盖然性：在这正在开启的一年里，一纸开拔令就可能把你从我怀抱里夺走。这已尽够使我焦虑和悲伤到发狂了。」
「你想想看，玛尔塔。你自己也正要迎着一场危险呢——你那件圣诞礼物已 charmingly 地把这事告诉了我——可我们俩并没有去想那悬在每个产妇头上的残酷可能，那危险约等于战场上每个男人所面对的。让我们享受生命，别去想那悬在我们所有人头上的死。」
「你说话像极了玛丽姨母，最亲爱的，好像我们的命运系于『天意』，而不是系于我们同胞的轻率、残忍、放纵和愚妄。这场对丹麦的战争，那不可避免的必要性究竟在哪里？」
「它还没有爆发，说不定还——」
「我知道，我知道；也许还会发生什么意外，把这灾祸岔开。可决定这类命运问题的，本不该是偶然，不该是政治的阴谋和意气；而该是人类坚定、正义的*意志*。可我这些『该』与『不该』又有什么用？我改变不了事物的秩序。我只能抱怨它。可你总要帮我到这一步，腓特烈！

===Original===

Do not try to console me with hollow conventional evasions! You do not believe in them yourself! You yourself are shuddering with noble repugnance! The only consolation I find is in thinking that you condemn and bewail as I do what will make me and numberless others so unhappy.”
“Yes, my dear; if this fatality should come to pass, then I will say you are right. Then I will not hide from you the shuddering and the hate which the national slaughter ordained on us awakes in me. But today let us still enjoy our life. We surely have each other﻿—nothing separates us. There is not the slightest bar between our souls! Let us enjoy this happiness as long as we have it; enjoy it to the full. Let us not think of the threatened destruction of it. No joy assuredly can last forever. In a hundred years it will be all the same whether our life has been long or short. The number of beautiful days is not the question, but the degree of their beauty. Let the future bring what it pleases, my dearly-loved wife; our present is so beautiful, so very beautiful, that I cannot now feel anything but a blessed delight.”
As he said this, he threw his arm around me, and kissed my head, which rested on his breast. And then the threatening future disappeared for me also, and I too let myself sink into the sweet transport of the moment.
---
On 10th January we returned to Olmütz.
No one any longer doubted about the outbreak of war. I had heard a few individuals in Vienna hope that the Schleswig-Holstein dispute could even yet be capable of diplomatic settlement; but in the military circles of our garrison town all possibility of peace was held to be out of the question. Among the officers and their wives there prevailed an excited, but on the whole joyfully excited, temper. Opportunities for distinction and advancement were in prospect, for the satisfaction of the love of adventure in one, the ambition of another, the thirst for promotion of a third.
“This is a famous war which is in prospect,” said the colonel, to whose house, with several other officers and their wives, we were invited to dinner; “a famous war, and one that must be immensely popular. No danger to our territory; and even the population of our country will suffer no diminution, since the scene of war lies on foreign soil.”

===Chinese===

别拿空洞的场面话来安慰我！那些话你自己也不信！你自己也在高贵的憎恶中战栗！我唯一的安慰，就是想到你和我一样，谴责、哀恸着那将使我和无数人如此不幸的东西。」
「是，亲爱的；倘若这劫数真的临头，我就承认你有理。到那时我绝不向你隐瞒：这场强加给我们的民族屠杀在我心里唤起的战栗与憎恨。可今天，让我们仍然享受我们的生命。我们确确实实拥有着彼此——没有什么能把我们分开。我们两颗灵魂之间没有一丝一毫的隔阂！趁着还拥有这幸福，让我们享受它；尽情地享受它。别去想那对它的威胁和毁灭。确实没有一种欢乐能永远长存。一百年之后，我们的命长命短，横竖都一样。问题不在美好日子的数目，而在它们美好的程度。随未来带来什么吧，我深爱的妻子；我们的现在是这么美，这么美，以致此刻我心里只容得下一种蒙福的欢悦。」
他说着，搂住我，吻着我靠在他胸前的头。于是那咄咄逼人的未来对我也消失了，我也让自己沉入了此刻甜蜜的迷醉。
---
1月10日我们回到奥尔米茨。
再没有人怀疑战争的爆发了。我曾在维也纳听个别人士指望石勒苏益格-荷尔斯泰因争端还有希望通过外交解决；可在我们这个驻防城镇的军人圈子里，一切和平的可能都被认为无从谈起。军官们和他们的太太中间弥漫着一种激动的、而且总体上是欢欣鼓舞的情绪。建立功勋和获得晋升的机会在望，可以满足这个人的冒险欲、那个人的雄心、第三个人的升迁渴。
「眼前的这是一场再好不过的战争，」上校说——我们应邀到他府上，与另外几位军官及太太共进晚餐；「一场再好不过的战争，而且必定大得人心。我们的领土没有危险；连我们国家的人口也不会有折损，因为战场远在外国土地上。」

===Original===

“What inspires me in the matter,” said a young first lieutenant, “is the noble motive, to defend the rights of our brethren under oppression. The fact that the Prussians are marching with us﻿—or rather we with them﻿—assures us in the first place of victory, and in the next place it will bind still closer the bonds of nationality. The national idea﻿—”
“I had rather you would not talk about that,” interposed the colonel rather sternly. “That humbug does not sit well on an Austrian. It was that that raised up the Italian war against us; for it was on this hobbyhorse, ‘Italy for the Italians,’ that Louis Napoleon kept always mounting, and the whole principle is specially unsuitable for Austria. Bohemians, Hungarians, Germans, Croats﻿—where is the bond of nationality? We know one principle only which unites us, and that is a loyal love of our reigning family. Therefore, what ought to put spirit into us when we take the field is not the circumstance that we are Germans, and have Germans as allies, but that we can render loyal service to our exalted and beloved commander-in-chief. The emperor’s health!”
All stood up to drink the toast. A spark of animation even reached my heart, inflaming it for a moment and filling it with a warmth that did me good. That thousands should love one and the same cause, one and the same person, is a thing which produces a peculiar, a thousandfold impulse of devotion. And that is the feeling which swells the heart under the name of loyalty, patriotism, or esprit-de-corps. It is in reality nothing but love; and this has such a mighty working that a man regards the work of hatred ordained in its name, even the most horrible work of the deadliest hatred﻿—War﻿—as the fulfilment of the duty of his love.
But this glow only lasted in my heart for one instant, for a love stronger than that for any earthly fatherland or father of the country filled its depths﻿—the love of my husband. *His* life was to me in all cases the dearest of my possessions, and if *it* was to be the stake I could do nothing but abhor the game, whether it was to be played for Schleswig-Holstein or Japan.
The time which now followed I passed in unspeakable anxiety.

===Chinese===

「鼓舞我投入这一仗的，」一位年轻的骑兵中尉说，「是那高尚的动机：捍卫受压迫的同胞的权利。普鲁士人和我们并肩进军——或者不如说我们和他们并肩——这一事实首先保证了胜利，其次还会把民族的纽带系得更紧。民族的思想——」
「这个话题我宁愿你别谈，」上校相当严厉地插了一句。「那套把戏穿在奥地利人身上不合身。正是它惹来了意大利那场战争对我们的围攻；路易·拿破仑骑的就是『意大利人的意大利』这匹木马，一遍又一遍；而这条原则对奥地利尤其不合适。波希米亚人、匈牙利人、德意志人、克罗地亚人——民族纽带在哪里？我们只知道一条把我们联结在一起的原则，那就是对我们皇室忠诚的爱。因此，激励我们上阵的，不应当是我们是德意志人、有德意志人做盟友这一层，而是我们能够为我们崇高而敬爱的总司令效犬马之劳。皇帝万岁！」
全体起立举杯。振奋的火星甚至窜进了我的心，一时把它点燃，使它充满一股令我受用的暖意。千万人热爱着同一桩事业、同一个人，这件事会产生一种奇特的、千倍增涨的献身冲动。那便是被称为忠诚、爱国或团队精神、在胸中鼓荡的那种感情。它其实不外是爱；而爱的力量如此强大，以致人会把以爱之名安排下来的仇恨的作业——连最致命的仇恨那最可怕的作业——战争——都看作他爱的义务的履行。
可这股热焰在我心里只燃了一瞬，因为一种比对尘世的任何祖国或国父更强烈的爱占据着我的心底——对我丈夫的爱。*他的*生命在任何情形下都是我最珍贵的所有，倘若押上作注的竟是*它*，那我便只有憎恶这场赌局一途，无论赌的是石勒苏益格-荷尔斯泰因还是日本。
接下来的这段日子，我是在难以言喻的焦虑中度过的。

===Original===

On 16th January the powers of the Bund addressed a demand to Denmark calling on her to abrogate a certain law, against which the Convocation of Estates and the nobles of Holstein had invoked the protection of the Bund, and to do this in twenty-four hours. Denmark refused. Who would consent to be commanded in that fashion? This refusal had been foreseen, of course, for Austrian and Prussian troops stood ready posted on the frontier; and on 1st February they crossed the Eider.
So the bloody die was cast again﻿—the game had begun. This gave occasion to my father to send us a letter of congratulation.
“Rejoice, my children,” he wrote. “Now we have at length an opportunity to repair the losses we got in ’59, by inflicting losses on the Danes. When we have come back from the north as conquerors, we shall be able to turn our faces southwards again. The Prussians will remain our constant allies; and in that case these shabby Italians and their intriguing Louis Napoleon cannot again stand up against us.”
Frederick’s regiment, to the great disappointment of the colonel and the corps of officers, was not despatched to the frontier. This fact brought us a paternal letter of condolence:﻿—

> “I am heartily sorry that Tilling has the ill-luck to be serving in just one of the regiments which are not called on to open the campaign which has such glorious prospects, but there remains always the possibility that he will be marked out to follow in support. Martha, indeed, will look on the best side of the business, and be glad that the fear for her beloved husband is spared her, and Frederick also is confessedly no friend of war; but I think he is only against it in principle, that is to say, he would rather, on grounds of so-called ‘humanity,’ that it should never come to fighting, but when it has so come, then he would, I know, rather have a part in it, for then I know his manly love of battle would awake. In truth it ought to be the *whole* army that should always be sent to meet the foe; at such a time to be forced to stay at home is surely something altogether too hard on a soldier.”

===Chinese===

1月16日，邦联各强国向丹麦发出通牒，要求它废除一项法令——邦联议会和荷尔斯泰因贵族曾就这项法令请求邦联的保护——限二十四小时内照办。丹麦拒绝了。谁肯听人用这种口气发号施令？这一拒绝当然早在意料之中，因为奥地利和普鲁士的军队早已整装待发、陈兵边境；2月1日，他们渡过了艾德河。
血淋淋的骰子又一次掷下——赌局开场了。这给了父亲一个由头，给我们寄来一封道贺信。
「欢欣吧，孩子们，」他写道。「我们终于有机会收拾丹麦人，好补回五九年受的损失了。等我们以征服者的身份从北方回来，我们就可以再掉头南向。普鲁士人将始终是我们的盟友；到那时，那些寒酸的意大利人和他们那个惯弄权谋的路易·拿破仑，就再也不能与我们作对了。」
使上校和全团军官大失所望的是，腓特烈的团没有被派往边境。这一事实给我们招来一封慈父般的慰问信：——

> 「蒂林竟在恰恰不被征调参加这场前景如此辉煌的战役的团队里任职，我由衷地替他惋惜；不过他仍有可能被点中随后增援。玛尔塔当然会往好里看这件事，会庆幸免去了为亲爱的丈夫担惊受怕，而腓特烈公认也不是战争之友；可我想他只是原则上反对战争，也就是说，基于所谓的『人道』，他宁愿永远打不起来；可一旦真打了起来，据我所知，他倒宁可躬与其事，因为那时他那种男子汉的战斗欲就会醒来。说实在的，御敌的理应永远是*全军*；在那样的时候被迫留在家里，对一个军人来说未免太难受了。」

===Original===

“Does it strike you as hard, my Frederick, to remain with me?” I asked, after reading the letter.
He pressed me to his heart. The dumb reply contented me.
But what was the good of it? My peace was gone. The order to march might come any day. If the unhappy war could only be brought to an end quickly! With the greatest eagerness did I read in the newspapers the news from the seat of war, and warmly did I wish that the allies might win speedy and decisive victories. I confess that the wish had no patriotism at all in it. I should indeed have preferred that the victory should be on our side; but what I hoped from it was the termination of the war, before my “all on earth” was out there; and then only in the second degree the triumph of my countrymen, and quite in the last the “sea-surrounded” patch of country. Whether, however, Schleswig was to belong to Denmark or no, what in the world could that matter to me? And finally, what matter could it make to the Danes and Schleswig-Holsteiners themselves? Could not then the two nations themselves see that it was only their rulers who were quarrelling about the possession of territory and power, and that in the present case, for example, the question was not their good or their suffering, but the wishes of the so-called Prince “Protocol” and of the Augustenburgs? If a number of dogs are fighting over some bones, it is still only the dogs themselves who tear each other; but in the history of nations it is chiefly the poor silly bones themselves that rush at each other and knock each other to pieces on the two sides, in fighting for the rights of the combatants who covet them. “Lion wants me,” or “Towser has a claim on me.” “I protest against Caro’s fangs,” or “I reckon it an honour to be swallowed by Growler,” cry the bones. “Denmark up to the Eider,” shouted the Danish patriots. “We will have Frederick of Augustenburg for our duke,” shouted the loyalists of Holstein. The articles in our papers and the talk of our quidnuncs were all of course permeated by the principle that the cause for which “we” had entered into the war was the right one, the only one which was “historically developed”﻿—the only one necessary for the maintenance of “the balance of power in Europe.” And of course the opposite principle was maintained with equal emphasis in the leading articles and the political speeches in Copenhagen.

===Chinese===

「留在我们身边，你觉得难受吗，我的腓特烈？」读完信，我问他。
他把我搂在心头。这无声的回答让我满足了。
可这又顶什么用呢？我的安宁没有了。开拔令随时可能到来。这场不幸的战争要是能快点结束才好！我怀着最大的热忱读着报纸上来自战区的消息，热切盼望联军赢得迅速而决定性的胜利。我承认这愿望里没有半点爱国心。胜利在我们这边，这我确实更愿意；可我指望于它的，是趁我的「身家性命所系」还没有开到那边之前，战争就告结束；其次才是同胞的凯旋，最后才轮到那块「四面环海」的巴掌大的地方。至于石勒苏益格归丹麦还是不归，与我又有什么相干？说到底，它与丹麦人、与石勒苏益格-荷尔斯泰因人自己又有什么相干？难道这两国人民自己就看不见，争吵着争夺领土和权势的只是他们的君主，而眼下这桩公案里，问题根本不在他们的福祉或苦难，而在那位所谓的「议定书亲王」和奥古斯滕堡家族的意愿？一群狗争骨头，撕咬的毕竟只是狗自己；可在民族的历史上， chiefly 竟是那些可怜的傻骨头自己冲上前去、在两边替觊觎它们的交战者的权利互相撕碎彼此。「狮子要得我，」或者「托泽对我有主权。」「我抗议卡罗的獠牙，」或者「能被格罗勒吞吃我引以为荣，」骨头们喊道。「丹麦的疆界到艾德河！」丹麦的爱国者喊。「我们要奥古斯滕堡的腓特烈做我们的公爵！」荷尔斯泰因的保王党喊。我们报纸上的文章和好事者的谈论，自然全都渗透着这样一条原则：「我们」参战所捍卫的事业是正当的，是唯一「历史地发展出来的」事业——是维持「欧洲均势」唯一必需的事业。而当然，哥本哈根的社论和政界演说，又以同等的力度坚持着恰好相反的原则。

===Original===

Why not on both sides weigh the rival claims, in order to come to an understanding; and if this should fail, make a third power arbitrator? Why go on always shouting on both sides, “I, I am in the right”﻿—and even shouting it out against one’s own conviction, till one has shouted oneself hoarse, and finishes by leaving the decision to *Force*? Is not that savagery? And even should a third power mix in the strife, it also does so, not with a balancing of rights or a judicial sentence, but equally with downright blows! And that is what people call “foreign politics.” Foreign and domestic savagery it is﻿—statesmanlike tomfoolery﻿—international barbarism!
---
It is true that I did not at that time look at what was going on in this light with such certainty as this. It was only for a few moments that doubts of this sort woke up in me, and then I took all possible pains to chase them away. I attempted to persuade myself that the mysterious thing called “reasons of state,” a thing elevated above all private reason, and particularly my own poor faculties, was a principle on which the life of states depends, and I began a zealous study of the history of Schleswig-Holstein, in order to arrive at a conception of the “historic rights” which it was the object of the present proceedings to maintain.
And then I discovered that the strip of land in dispute had, as early as the year 1027, been ceded to Denmark. So, in reality, the Danes are in the right. They are the legitimate kings of the country.
But then, 200 years later, the district was made over to a younger branch of the royal house, and then ranked rather as a fief of the Danish crown. In 1326 Schleswig was given over to Count Gerhard of Holstein, and “the Constitution of Waldemar” provides that “it should never again be so far united with Denmark that there should be but one lord.” Oh! then the right is still on the side of the allies. We are fighting for the Constitution of Waldemar. That is quite correct, for what is the use of these securities on paper if they are not to be upheld?
In the year 1448 the Constitution of Waldemar was again confirmed by King Christian I. So there can be no doubt that there must and shall never again be “one lord.” What has the Protocol-Prince to do in the matter?

===Chinese===

为什么不双方都把各自的权利主张摆上天平，以求达成谅解；万一不成，何不请第三国仲裁？为什么总是两边一味叫嚷「我，我才有理」——甚至叫嚷到违背自己的信念，直到嗓子喊哑，末了把裁决交给*武力*？这难道不是野蛮？而且即便真有第三国插手争端，它来时拿的也不是衡量权利的天平或一纸判决，而同样是劈头盖脸的拳头！而这竟被称作「外交」。这是对外的和对内的野蛮——是政治家的愚蠢把戏——是国际的蒙昧！
---
的确，当时我还没有这样肯定地用这样的眼光看待眼前发生的一切。这类怀疑只是偶尔在我心中苏醒片刻，随后我便千方百计把它们赶开。我试图说服自己：那个叫做「国家理由」的神秘东西——它高悬于一切私人的理性之上，尤其高悬于我自己可怜的悟性之上——是一条国家生命所系的原则；于是我开始热切地研读石勒苏益格-荷尔斯泰因的历史，想对此次行动所要维护的「历史权利」求得一个概念。
于是我发现了，那条有争议的土地早在1027年就已割让给丹麦。这么说，实际上丹麦人有理。他们才是这个国家合法的君王。
可是两百年后，这块地盘又划给了王室的一个幼支，此后与其说是丹麦王冠的采邑。1326年，石勒苏益格被授予荷尔斯泰因的格哈德伯爵，而「瓦尔德马尔宪章」规定：「它今后与丹麦的合并，永不得至于只余一位君主之境。」哦！那么道理还是在同盟这一边。我们是为瓦尔德马尔宪章而战。这完全正当，因为纸上的这些保证若不去维护，还要它们何用？
1448年，瓦尔德马尔宪章又得到克里斯蒂安一世的重新确认。那么毫无疑问，永远、永远不该再出现「一位君主」。议定书亲王在这里面有什么干系？

===Original===

Twelve years later, the ruler of Schleswig dies without issue, and the Estates of the country meet at Ripen (it would be well if we always knew with such exactness when and where the Estates met﻿—well, it was in 1460 at Ripen), and they proclaim the King of Denmark Duke of Schleswig, in return for which he promises them that the countries “shall remain together forever, undivided.” This makes me again a little confused. The only point to hold by is that they “shall remain together forever.”
But the confusion goes on constantly increasing, as this historical study takes a wider circuit; for now in spite of the formula “forever undivided” (the word “forever” plays an exquisite part generally in political business), there commences an everlasting cutting up and division of the territory amongst the king’s sons and a reunion of these under a succeeding king, and the founding of new families, Holstein-Gottorp and Schleswig-Sonderburg, which with reciprocal shuffling and cessions of their shares, again separate themselves into the families of Sonderburg-Augustenburg, Beck-Glücksburg, Sonderburg-Glücksburg, Holstein-Glückstadt. In short, I no longer knew where I was.
But there is more to come. Perhaps the “historical claim” for which the sons of our country have to bleed today may not have been established till later.
Christian IV mixed himself up in the Thirty Years’ War, and the Imperialists and Swedes invaded the duchies. Now was made (at Copenhagen, 1658) another treaty, by which the lordship over the Schleswig portion was secured to the house of Holstein Gottorp, and so at last we have got done with the Danish feudal lordship. Done with it forever. Thank God. Now I find myself again all right.
But what happened by the Patent of 22nd August, 1721? Simply this: the Gottorps’ dominion of Schleswig was incorporated into the kingdom of Denmark. In January, 1773, Holstein also was ceded to the royal house of Denmark; the whole ranked now as a Danish province.
That changes the affair, the Danes are in the right.
Yet not entirely so. The Congress of Vienna, in 1815, declares Holstein to be a part of the German Bund. This, however, vexes the Danes.

===Chinese===

十二年后，石勒苏益格的君主死后无嗣，邦国的等级会议在里本集会（但愿我们总能这样确切地知道等级会议于何时何地召开——好吧，那是1460年，在里本），他们宣告丹麦国王为石勒苏益格公爵，国王则报以承诺：两国「将永不分离，永相结合」。这又使我糊涂了一点。唯一抓得住的要点是「将永相结合」。
可是，随着这项历史研究越铺越宽，糊涂也越闹越大；因为如今，尽管有「永远不分离」的公式（「永远」这个词在政治买卖里素来扮演着精妙角色），那片领土却开始在历代王子之间无休止地分割，又在继任国王之下重新合一，还分出了新的家族支系：荷尔斯泰因-戈托普和石勒苏益格-森讷堡，它们经过彼此的倒手和份额的让与，又再析出森讷堡-奥古斯滕堡、贝克-格吕克斯堡、森讷堡-格吕克斯堡、荷尔斯泰因-格吕克施塔特诸家。简而言之，我已经不知道自己身在何处了。
可还有下文。或许今天要我国之子民为之流血的这条「历史权利」，建立得还要更晚。
克里斯蒂安四世卷入了三十年战争，帝国军和瑞典人侵入了两公国。于是又订了一项条约（1658年，哥本哈根），把石勒苏益格部分的领主权确保给荷尔斯泰因-戈托普家族，这样我们总算摆脱了丹麦的封建领主权。永远摆脱了。感谢上帝。这下我又站住脚了。
可是1721年8月22日的专利特许状又干了什么？简简单单：戈托普家在石勒苏益格的统治并入了丹麦王国。1773年1月，荷尔斯泰因也割让给丹麦王室；整个地区从此算作丹麦的一个省。
这就改变了局面，丹麦人有理。
然而也不尽然。1815年的维也纳会议宣布荷尔斯泰因为德意志邦联的一部分。这可惹恼了丹麦人。

===Original===

They invent the cry: “Denmark up to the Eider,” and struggle for the complete possession of Schleswig﻿—called by them “South Jutland,” against which the “hereditary right of Augustenburg” was employed as a watchword and used in German national proclamations. In the year 1846 King Christian writes a public letter in which he proposes the integrity of the entire state as his object, and against this “the German countries” protest. Two years later the complete union is announced from the Throne, no longer as an object, but as a fait accompli, and then the uprising occurs in the “German countries.” And now the fighting begins. At first the Danes gain the victory in one fight, next the Schleswig-Holsteiners in a second. Then the German Bund intervenes. The Prussians “occupy” the heights of Düppel, but that does not terminate the strife. Prussia and Denmark make peace. Schleswig-Holstein has now to fight the Danes single-handed, and is struck down at Idstedt.
The Bund now calls on the “revolters” to discontinue the war, which they proceed to do. Austrian troops take possession of Holstein, and the two duchies are *separated*. So what has become of the paper-stipulation “to be forever united”?
Still the situation is not made completely secure. Now I find a Protocol of London, 8th May, 1852 (it is a good thing that we always know so exactly the date when these fragile treaties are made), which secures the succession of Schleswig to Prince Christian of Glücksburg (“secures” is good). And now I know at any rate the origin of the name “Protocol-Prince.”
In the year 1854, after each duchy had received a constitution of its own, both were “Danised.” But in 1858 the Danisation of Holstein had to be revoked again. And now this historical sketch is coming quite close to the present time; and yet it is not so clear to me to whom the two countries “rightly belong,” or what was the precise cause of the outbreak of the present war.
On 18th November, 1858, the famous “Fundamental law for the mutual relations between Denmark and Schleswig” was passed by the Reichsrath. Two days afterwards the king died.

===Chinese===

他们发明了「丹麦的疆界到艾德河」的口号，为完全占有石勒苏益格——他们称之为「南日德兰」——而斗争；与之相对，「奥古斯滕堡的世袭权利」被用作口号，写进德意志的民族文告。1846年，克里斯蒂安国王写了一封公开信，提出以整个国家的完整统一为目标，对此「德意志邦国」提出抗议。两年后，完全的合并由王座谕示宣布，不再作为目标，而是既成事实；于是「德意志邦国」起义了。接着战端开启。起初丹麦人在一役中获胜，继而石勒苏益格-荷尔斯泰因人在另一役中取胜。于是德意志邦联出面干涉。普鲁士人「占领」了迪佩尔高地，但争端并未就此了结。普鲁士与丹麦媾和。石勒苏益格-荷尔斯泰因从此只得单枪匹马对付丹麦人，在伊德施泰特被击溃。
邦联随即要求「造反者」停战，他们照办了。奥地利军队占领荷尔斯泰因，两公国被*分开*了。那么，「永相结合」的纸上规定落到哪里去了？
局势仍未获得完全的保障。如今我又找到一份1852年5月8日的伦敦议定书（好在这些一碰就碎的条约订立的日期，我们总是知道得这么确切），它把石勒苏益格的王位继承权「确保」给格吕克斯堡的克里斯蒂安亲王（「确保」二字用得好）。至此我总算知道了「议定书亲王」这个名号的来历。
1854年，两公国各自获得一部宪法之后，双双被「丹麦化」。可1858年，荷尔斯泰因的丹麦化又不得不撤销。至此，这幅历史速写已经画到眼下的时光；可是这两块地方「究竟归属何人」，或者这场战争的真正起因是什么，我仍旧不甚了然。
1858年11月18日，著名的「丹麦与石勒苏益格相互关系基本法」由 Reichsrath 通过。两天之后，国王驾崩。

===Original===

With him again was extinguished a family﻿—that of Holstein-Glückstadt﻿—and when the successor of the monarch presented himself on the scene, in reliance on the two-days-old law, Frederick of Augustenburg (a family I had nearly forgotten) raised his claim, and together with his nobility turned for support to the German Bund.
The latter at once occupied Holstein with Saxon and Hanoverian troops, and proclaimed Augustenburg duke. Why? But Prussia and Austria were not of accord in this proceeding. Why? That I do not to this day understand.
It is said the London Protocol had to be respected. Why? Are these Protocols about things which concern us absolutely nothing so exceedingly to be respected, that we must defend them at the price of the blood of our own sons? If so, there must lie in the background some mysterious “reason of state” for it. It must be firmly held as a dogma that what the gentlemen round the green table of diplomacy may decide is the highest wisdom, and has for its aim the greatest possible advance of the power of one’s country. The London Protocol of 8th May, 1852, had to be maintained intact; but the Fundamental Law of Copenhagen, of 13th January, 1863, had to be abolished, and that within twenty-four hours. On that hung Austria’s honour and welfare. The dogma was a little hard to believe, but in political matters, almost more willingly than in religious, the masses allow themselves to be led by the principle of the “*quia absurdum*”﻿—they have renounced beforehand the attempt to reason and understand. When the sword is once drawn nothing more is necessary than to shout “Hurrah,” and press hotly on to victory. Besides that, all that is necessary is to invoke the blessing of heaven on the war. For so much is certain, that it must be the business of the Almighty to see that the Protocol of the 8th May is maintained, and the Law of 5th November repealed. He must conduct the matter so that the precise number of men bleed to death and villages are set on fire, that are necessary in order that the family of Glückstadt, or that of Augustenburg should rule over a particular spot of earth. What a foolish world﻿—still in leading strings﻿—cruel, unthinking! Such was the result of my historical studies.

===Chinese===

随着他，又一支家族熄灭了——荷尔斯泰因-格吕克施塔特家；当君主的继任人登场时，奥古斯滕堡的腓特烈（这个家族我险些忘了）依据那部才通过两天的法律提出了自己的权利要求，并连同他的贵族一齐向德意志邦联求援。
邦联当即以萨克森和汉诺威的军队占领荷尔斯泰因，宣告奥古斯滕堡为公爵。为什么？可普鲁士和奥地利不赞成这一做法。为什么？这我至今不明白。
据说伦敦议定书必须得到尊重。为什么？这些全然与我们无关的事情上的议定书，竟尊贵到必须用我们自己儿子的血去捍卫吗？倘若如此，背后必得藏着某种神秘的「国家理由」。必须把这样一条奉为教义：外交绿桌周围的诸位先生们所议定的，乃是至高的智慧，其目标就是本国权势最大可能的增进。1852年5月8日的伦敦议定书必须保持完整无损；而哥本哈根1863年1月13日的基本法却必须废除，而且限二十四小时内废除。奥地利的荣誉与福祉系于此。这条教义有点难于置信，可在政治事务里，民众几乎比在宗教事务里更甘愿受「*quia absurdum*」原则的引领——他们事先就放弃了推究和理解的尝试。一旦剑已出鞘，剩下的只消高呼「万岁」，向胜利猛冲。此外所需的无非是祈求上天赐福于战争。因为有一点是笃定的：全能者自当料理妥当，让5月8日的议定书得以维持，11月5日的法令得以废除。他必须把事情安排得恰到好处，让恰好那么多的人流血致死、恰好那么多的村庄付之一炬，好叫格吕克施塔特家、或者奥古斯滕堡家统治大地上某一个特定的点。多么愚蠢的世界啊——还在襁褓之中——残忍、不动脑筋！这便是我历史研究的结论。

## VII / 七
===Original===

The Course of the Danish War﻿—Suspension of Hostilities﻿—War Renewed﻿—My Husband Ordered Off Just on the Eve of My Confinement﻿—The Parting﻿—My Confinement Occurs Simultaneously with My Husband’s Departure﻿—A Dead Child﻿—The Mother in Deadly Peril﻿—Frederick’s Letters from the Seat of War﻿—Cousin Godfrey and the Alliance Between Austria and Prussia﻿—My Recovery﻿—Anxiety and Relapse﻿—Return of My Husband.
From the theatre of war came good tidings. The allies won battle after battle. Immediately after the first combats the Danes were forced to abandon the entire Danewerk. Schleswig and Jutland up to Limfjord were occupied by our troops, and the enemy only maintained himself in the lines at Düppel and at Alsen.
I knew all this so accurately, because on the tables were again laid the maps stuck about with pins on which were marked the movements and positions of the troops as each despatch arrived. “If we could now only take the lines at Düppel, or if we could even conquer Alsen,” said the citizens of Olmütz (for no one is so fond of speaking of deeds of war with the “we” as those who were never present at them), “then we should be at an end of it. Now our Austrians are showing again what they can do. The brave Prussians too are fighting splendidly. Both together are of course invincible. The end will be that all Denmark will be overrun and will be annexed to the German Bund﻿—a glorious, beneficent war.”
I too wished for nothing so anxiously as the storming of Düppel﻿—the sooner, the better﻿—for this action would at any rate be decisive and put an end to the butchery. Put an end to it, I hoped, before Frederick’s regiment got marching orders.
Oh, this Damocles’ sword! Every day when I woke the fear came on me that the news would be brought “We are to march.” Frederick was calm about it. He did not wish it, but saw it coming.
“Accustom yourself, dear, to the thought of it,” he said to me. “Against inexorable necessity no striving is of any avail. I do not believe that even if Düppel falls the war will thereby terminate. The allied army which has been despatched is far too small to force the Danes to a conclusion; we shall be obliged to send considerable reinforcements besides, and then my regiment will not be spared.”
In fact, this campaign had lasted more than two months, and yet no result. If the cruel game could have been settled in one fight like a duel!

===Chinese===

丹麦战争的进程——停战——战事重开——临盆前夕丈夫奉命开拔——诀别——我的分娩与丈夫的启程同日而至——死婴——母亲命悬一线——腓特烈战地来信——戈特弗里德表弟与奥普同盟——我的康复——焦虑与反复——丈夫归来。
战场上传来好消息。联军一场接一场地打赢。头几仗刚过，丹麦人就被迫放弃了整条丹内维尔克防线。石勒苏益格和日德兰直到利姆峡湾都被我军占领，敌人只据守着迪佩尔和阿尔森的阵地。
这一切我知道得如此确切，因为桌上又摊开了插满大头针的地图，每来一份战报就在上面标出部队的调动与位置。「咱们这会儿要是能拿下迪佩尔阵地，哪怕干脆把阿尔森也夺过来，」奥尔米茨（Olmütz）的市民们说（谈论战功时用「咱们」用得最起劲的，正是从未亲临战阵的人），「那这事就了啦。咱们奥地利人这回又要露一手了。勇敢的普鲁士人也打得出色。两家合在一起当然所向无敌。到头来整个丹麦都要被踏平，并入德意志邦联——一场辉煌的、造福于人的战争。」
我急切盼望的也莫过于强攻迪佩尔——越快越好——因为这一仗至少是决定性的，能给这场屠杀一个了结。赶在腓特烈的团接到开拔令之前了结它，我希望。
唉，这把达摩克利斯之剑！每天一醒来，恐惧便袭上心头：怕有人来报「我们要开拔了」。腓特烈对此很平静。他不愿如此，但看得到它的到来。
「亲爱的，让自己习惯这个念头吧，」他对我说。「对抗无情的必然，一切挣扎都无济于事。我不相信迪佩尔一陷落战争就会就此终结。已经派出去的联军兵力太小，不足以迫丹麦人就范；我们将不得不加派相当数量的增援，到那时我的团是免不了的。」
事实上，这场战役已经打了两个多月，却还毫无结果。这残忍的赌局若能像一场决斗那样一仗定输赢就好了！

===Original===

But no; if one battle is lost, another is offered; if one position has to be given up, another is taken, and so on till one or the other army is annihilated, or both are exhausted.
At last, on 14th April, the lines of Düppel were stormed.
The news was received with such a shout of joy as if the recovered paradise had lain behind these lines. People embraced each other in the streets. “Don’t you know? Düppel﻿—Oh, our brave army! An unheard-of exploit. Now let all join in thanking God!” And there was singing of “Te Deums” in all the churches, and among the military choirmasters an industrious composition of “The Lines of Düppel March,” “Storm of Düppel Galop,” and so forth.
My husband’s comrades and their wives had, it is true, a drop of bitterness in their cup of joy, not to have been there, to have been obliged to miss such a triumph; what bad luck!
This victory gave me one great joy, for immediately after it a peace conference assembled in London and occasioned a suspension of hostilities. What a recovery of free breath even that word “suspension of hostilities” caused.
How the world would at last breathe again, thought I then for the first time, if on all hands could be heard: “Lay down your arms,” down with them forever! I put the words into my red book, but beside them I wrote despondingly in brackets “Utopia.”
That the London Congress would make an end of the Schleswig-Holstein War I made no doubt at all. The allies had won, the lines of Düppel were carried, these lines had played so great a part in recent times that their capture seemed to me to be finally decisive: how could Denmark hold out longer? The negotiations dragged on for an incredible length of time. This would have been torture to me if I had not from the very beginning had the conviction that their result must be peaceful. If the plenipotentiaries of great states, who therefore must be reasonable, well-meaning persons, unite together to attain so desirable an end as the conclusion of peace, how could it fail? So much the more horribly was I undeceived when after debates continued for two months the news came that the congress had dissolved without accomplishing anything.
And two days later came marching orders for Frederick!
For preparations and for leave-taking he had twenty-four hours given him. And I was on the point of my confinement.

===Chinese===

可是不；一场败了，还有另一场奉上；一处阵地不得不放弃，就再占一处，如此以往，直到这一军或那一军被歼灭，或者两败俱伤。
终于，4月14日，迪佩尔阵地被强攻拿下。
消息迎来的是那样一阵欢呼，仿佛收复的乐园就藏在那道工事后面。人们在大街上互相拥抱。「您听说了吗？迪佩尔——哦，我们英勇的军队！前所未闻的奇功。大家都来感谢上帝吧！」于是各处教堂里唱起了《感恩赞美歌》，随军的乐正们则勤勤恳恳地谱起《迪佩尔阵地进行曲》《强攻迪佩尔加洛普舞曲》等等。
我丈夫的战友们和他们的太太们的欢喜杯中，倒是掺着一滴苦酒：没能到场，不得不错过这样一场凯旋，多不走运！
这场胜利给了我一个大欢喜，因为紧接着，伦敦召开了一次和会，促成了停战。单是「停战」这个词，就已让人多么畅快地喘过一口气来。
倘若四面八方都能听到「放下武器！」，永远放下——那时世界将终于怎样地重新呼吸啊，我生平第一次这样想。我把这几个字写进了我的红皮日记（本子）里，可在旁边又灰心地加了个括号：「乌托邦」。
伦敦和会将终结石勒苏益格-荷尔斯泰因（Schleswig-Holstein）战争，对此我毫不怀疑。联军赢了，迪佩尔阵地被攻克，这道工事在晚近的年代里扮演过那么重要的角色，它的陷落在我看来已是最终的决定：丹麦还怎么支撑得下去？谈判拖得叫人难以置信地长。倘若我不是从一开始就笃信其结果必定是和平，这对我就是一场酷刑。大国的全权代表们——因而必是些讲道理、怀善意的人——联合起来追求缔和这样一个求之不得的目标，怎么会不成功呢？于是，当辩论持续两个月之后传来和会一无所成而散会的消息时，我被惊醒得格外惨痛。
而两天之后，腓特烈的开拔令到了！
留给他做准备和道别的时间是二十四小时。而我，正临盆在即。

===Original===

In the heavy death-menacing hours, when a woman’s only comfort lies in having her dear husband by her, I had to remain alone, alone with that consciousness awful beyond everything that this dear husband was gone to the war﻿—knowing too that it must be just as painful to him to leave his poor wife at such a moment as it would be painful to me to be without him.
It was in the morning of 20th June. All the details of this memorable day remain impressed on my memory. Oppressive heat prevailed outside, and to shut this out the Venetian blinds had been let down in my room. Covered with light, loose clothing, I was lying exhausted on the sofa. I had passed an almost sleepless night, and had now shut my eyes in a dreamy half-doze. Near me on my table was standing a vase with some powerfully smelling roses. Through the open window the sound of a distant exercise in trumpet-playing came in. Everything was provocative of slumber, yet consciousness had not quite left me. Only one half of it﻿—I mean that of care﻿—had departed. I had forgotten the danger of war and the danger that stood before myself. I knew only that I was alive﻿—that the roses, along with the rhythm of the reveille which the trumpeter was playing, were giving out sweet soothing influences﻿—that my beloved husband might come in at any minute, and if he saw me asleep would only tread in the lightest manner so as not to awaken me. I was right; next minute the door opposite to me opened. Without raising my lids I could see through a tiny cleft between the eyelashes that it was he whom I was expecting. I made no attempt to rouse myself from my half-slumber, for by doing so I might chase away the whole picture; for it might be that the appearance at the door was only the continuation of a dream, and it might be that I was only dreaming that I had opened my eyelids ever so little. So now I shut them entirely and took pains to continue the dream﻿—that the dear one came closer, that he bent over me and kissed my forehead.
And so indeed it was. Then he knelt down by my couch and remained motionless for a while. The roses were still breathing and the distant horn playing its *tra-ra-ra*.
“Martha, are you asleep?” I heard him ask softly.
Then I opened my eyes.
“For God’s sake, what is it?”

===Chinese===

在那样沉重、死亡的阴影步步紧逼的时辰里——女人的唯一安慰本是亲爱的丈夫守在身边——我却不得不独处，独自怀着那比一切都可怕的意识：这个亲爱的丈夫上战场去了——同时也知道，他在这样的时刻撇下可怜的妻子，必定和我失去他一样痛苦。
那是6月20日的早晨。这个难忘的日子的一切细节都烙在我的记忆里。外面暑气逼人，为了挡住它，我房里的软百叶帘都放了下来。我盖着轻薄宽松的衣裳，疲惫地躺在沙发上。我几乎一夜没合眼，此刻闭着眼，处在迷迷糊糊的半寐之中。我身边的桌上摆着一瓶香气浓烈的玫瑰。敞开的窗外传来远处练习号音的声音。一切都催人入睡，可知觉还没有全然离我而去。它只剩一半——我说的是牵挂的那一半——已经去了。我忘掉了战争的危险，也忘掉了悬在我自己面前的危险。我只知道自己活着——知道玫瑰正伴着号手吹奏的起床号节律，散发出甜柔的抚慰——知道我亲爱的丈夫随时可能进来，他若见我睡着，会放轻脚步生怕吵醒我。我想得不错；紧接着，我对面的门开了。不必抬眼皮，我就能从睫毛间的一道细缝里看出，来的正是我盼的人。我没有努力从半睡中醒转，因为一动也许会把整幅图景驱散；门口的那个身影，也许只是一场梦的延续，也许我只是梦见自己把眼皮睁开了一丝。于是我干脆把眼睛闭严，费劲地把这场梦续下去——亲爱的走近了，他俯下身来，吻我的前额。
梦果然成了真。他跪在我的卧榻旁，一动不动地待了一会儿。玫瑰仍在吐芳，远处的号角仍吹着它的*嗒—啦—啦—啦*。
「玛尔塔，你睡着了？」我听见他轻声问。
于是我睁开了眼睛。
「天哪，你怎么了？」

===Original===

I cried out, frightened to death, for the countenance of my husband as he knelt by me was so deeply overclouded by sorrow that I guessed at once that some misfortune had happened. Instead of replying he laid his head on my breast.
I understood all. He had to go. I had thrown my arm round his neck, and we remained both in the same position for some time without speaking.
“When?” I asked at length.
“Early tomorrow morning.”
“Oh, my God! my God!”
“Calm yourself, my poor Martha.”
“No, no, let me weep. My misfortune is too great, and I know﻿—I see it in your face﻿—so is yours. Never did I see so much pain in any human face as I have just read in your features.”
“Yes, my wife. I am unfortunate to have to leave you in such a moment﻿—”
“Frederick, Frederick; we shall never see each other again. I shall die﻿—”
“Or I shall fall. Yes, I believe it, too; we shall never see each other again!”
It was a heartbreaking parting that occupied these last twenty-four hours. This was now the second time in my life that I had seen a dear husband depart to the war. But this second tearing ourselves apart was incomparably worse than the first. Then my way of taking it and still more Arno’s was quite different and more primitive. I looked on the departure as a natural necessity which overbalanced all personal feelings, and he looked at it even as a joyous expedition in search of glory. He went with cheerfulness. I remained without a murmur. There still clung to me something of the admiration for war which I had imbibed from my youthful education. I still shared to some extent with the departing soldier in the pride which he visibly felt in the “great emprise.” But now I knew that he who was going went to the work of death with horror rather than with exultation, I knew that he loved the life which he had to set on the hazard﻿—that to him one thing was dearer than everything, yes, everything, even the claims of the Augustenburgs﻿—his wife﻿—his wife who in a few days was to be a mother. Whilst in Arno’s case I had the conviction that he departed with feelings for which he was surely to be envied, I discerned that in this second separation both of us were deserving of equal pity. Yes, we suffered in equal measure, and we confessed it and bewailed it to each other.

===Chinese===

我吓得要死地喊了出来，因为跪在我身边的丈夫脸上愁云密布，我立刻猜到出了什么不幸。他没有回答，只把头伏在我胸前。
我全明白了。他得走了。我早已搂住他的脖颈，我们俩就这样保持着同一个姿势，好一阵子谁也不说话。
「什么时候？」我终于问。
「明天一早。」
「哦，我的上帝！我的上帝！」
「平静些，我可怜的玛尔塔。」
「不，不，让我哭。我的不幸太大了，而且我知道——我从你脸上看得出——你的也一样。我从来没有在哪张人脸上见过像刚才在你五官上读到的那么多痛苦。」
「是，我的妻。我偏偏要在这样的时刻离开你，我真是不幸——」
「腓特烈，腓特烈；我们再也见不着了。我要死了——」
「或者我阵亡。是，我也相信；我们再也见不着了！」
这最后的二十四小时，被一场肝肠寸断的诀别占满了。这是我生平第二次目送亲爱的丈夫开赴战场。可这第二次的生离，比第一次残酷得不可同日而语。那时，我对这件事的态度，尤其是阿尔诺的态度，全然不同，也原始得多。我把开拔看作压倒一切个人情感的天经地义，他更把它当作一场寻觅荣耀的快意远征。他走时兴致高昂。我留下时没有一句怨言。我身上还粘着少年时代所受教养灌输给我的对战争的几分崇拜。我还多少分享着出征军人对这场「伟大功业」显然怀有的骄傲。可如今我知道，这个出走的人是怀着恐惧而非振奋去赴那死亡的作业的；我知道他爱着那不得不押上赌局的生命——对他来说有一样东西比一切都珍贵，是的，比一切都珍贵，连奥古斯滕堡家的权利要求也不例外——那就是他的妻子——几天之内就要做母亲的妻子。当年对阿尔诺，我曾深信他带着令人艳羡的心情离去；而这第二次分离，我看得出我们两人同样值得怜悯。是的，我们受着同等的苦，我们也彼此承认，彼此哀恸。

===Original===

No hypocrisies, no empty phrases of consolation, no swagger; we were one in all things, and neither sought to deceive the other. It was still our best consolation that each could fully understand the other’s inconsolability. We did not seek to conceal the magnitude of the misfortune that had burst on us by any conventional cloaks or masks of patriotism or heroism. No, the prospect of being allowed to shoot and hack at the Danes was to him no compensation for the anguish of having to leave me﻿—on the contrary, rather an aggravation﻿—for killing and destroying is repulsive to every “noble man.” And to me it was no recompense﻿—absolutely none﻿—for *my* suffering to think that my dear one might perhaps gain a step in rank. And should the misfortune of this perilous separation rise to the still greater misfortune of parting forever﻿—should Frederick fall﻿—the reasons of state on account of which this war had to be waged were not in the faintest degree elevated or holy enough to my mind to balance such a sacrifice. “Defender of his Country,” that is the fair-sounding title with which the soldier is decorated. And in fact what nobler duty can there be for the members of a commonwealth than to defend their state when menaced? But then why does his military oath bind the soldier to a hundred other warlike duties, besides the defensive? Why is he obliged to go and attack? Why must he, in cases where there is not the slightest menace of any invasion of his country, hazard the same possessions﻿—his life and his hearth﻿—in the quarrels of certain foreign princes for territory or ambition, as if it were a question, as it surely ought to be to justify war, of the defence of endangered life and hearth? Why, for example, in the present instance, must the Austrian army march out to set the Augustenburgs on a foreign throne? Why? Why? The question is one which to address to an emperor or pope is in itself treasonable and blasphemous, which in the latter case passes for irreligion and in the former for want of loyalty, and which never deserves an answer.
The regiment was to march at 10 a.m. We stayed up the whole night. Not a minute of the time still left to us to spend together would we lose.
There was so much that we had still to say to each other, and yet we spoke little.

===Chinese===

没有虚伪，没有空洞的安慰话，没有虚张声势；我们在一切上都是一体的，谁也不欺骗谁。我们最大的安慰仍是：彼此都能完全懂得对方的不可安慰。我们不去用爱国或英勇这类惯常的遮身布和假面具，掩饰砸到我们头上的不幸之大。不，获准向丹麦人开枪砍杀的前景，于他绝不是补偿离开我的痛苦——毋宁说更是一种加重——因为杀戮和毁坏令每一个「高贵的人」憎恶。而对我来说，想到亲人或许能升一级军阶，也丝毫——丝毫不能抵偿*我的*苦。倘若这凶险分离的不幸再升高为永诀的不幸——倘若腓特烈阵亡——那么，这场战争据以开打的那些国家理由，在我的天平上绝没有半分崇高或神圣，足以抵住这样的牺牲。「祖国的捍卫者」，这是加在军人身上动听的头衔。而且事实上，一个共同体的成员，在国难当头时起来保卫自己的国家，还有比这更高贵的义务吗？可是，军人的宣誓为什么除了守土之外，还要把他束缚于一百样别的战争义务？为什么他必须去进攻？为什么在祖国的遭受侵略没有丝毫威胁的情形下，他必须为几位外国君主的领土之争或野心之争，押上同样的所有——他的生命和他的家园——仿佛那真的是一场（战争若要正当，就理应如此）保卫危殆的生命与家园之战？比如眼下的例子，奥地利军队为什么必须开出去，把奥古斯滕堡家扶上一张外国的王座？为什么？为什么？这个问题，拿去问皇帝或教皇本身就是叛逆和亵渎，在后一种场合要被当作渎神，在前一种场合要被当作不忠，而且永远不配有回答。
团队定于上午10时开拔。我们整夜没睡。还留给我们共处的时光，一分一秒也不肯丢。
我们还有那么多话要彼此诉说，却说得很少。

===Original===

It was mainly kisses and tears, which said more plainly than any words: “I love you, and I have to leave you.” From time to time there dropped in a hopeful word, “When you come back again.” It was certainly possible. Surely there are so many that come back; yet it was strange I repeated “When you come back” and tried to put before myself the delights of this event; but in vain. My imagination could form no other picture than that of my husband’s corpse on the field of battle, or myself on the bier, with a dead child in my arms.
Frederick was filled with similar gloomy forebodings, for his “When I come back” did not sound natural; and more often he spoke of what might happen, “If I should fall.”
“Do not marry a third time, Martha! Do not wash out, by the impressions of a new love, the recollections of this glorious year! Has it not been a happy time?”
We now recalled a hundred little details which had impressed themselves on our minds, from our first meeting to the present hour, and passed them through our remembrance.
“And my little one, my poor little one, whom perhaps I may never press to my heart, what is its name to be?”
“Frederick or Frederica.”
“No; Martha is prettier. If it is a girl call it by the name which its dying father at the last moment﻿—”
“Frederick, why do you talk always about dying? If you come back﻿—”
“Ah! *if!*” he repeated with a sigh.
As the day was beginning to dawn, my eyes, weary with weeping, closed, a light slumber fell on both of us. We lay there with our arms linked together, but without losing the consciousness that this was our parting hour.
Suddenly I started up and broke out into loud groans. Frederick got up at once.
“In God’s name, Martha, what is the matter with you? It is not yet come? Oh speak! Is it﻿—”
I nodded affirmatively.
Was it a cry, or a curse, or an ejaculation of prayer, that escaped his lips? He clutched the bell and gave the alarm.
“Run at once for the doctor﻿—for the nurse,” he shouted to the maid who had hurried in. Then he threw himself down on his knees beside me, and kissed my hand as it hung down.
“My wife! my all! and *now, now* I have to go.”
I could not speak. The most violent physical pain that one can conceive was racking and wringing my body; and besides this, the agony of my soul was yet more horrible, that he “had to go *now, now*”; and that he was so wretched about it.

===Chinese===

那主要是吻和泪，它们比任何言语都更直白地说着：「我爱你，而我不得不离开你。」其间不时落进一句怀有希望的话：「等你回来的时候。」这当然是有可能的。回来的人有那么多呢；可怪就怪在，我一遍遍说着「等你回来」，却怎么也想象不出那件事的欢乐。我的想象力只拼凑得出两幅图景：一幅是我丈夫的尸身横在战场上，另一幅是我自己躺在灵床上，怀里抱着一个死去的孩子。
腓特烈心里也充满同样阴郁的预感，因为他那声「等我回来」听起来不自然；他更多地说着万一的话，「万一我阵亡了」。
「你可不要第三次结婚，玛尔塔！不要用一段新爱的印象，洗去这幸福一年的记忆！这一年难道不是美好的时光吗？」
我们此刻追忆起从初识到此时此刻印在心头的千百个细节，把它们一件件从记忆里过了一遍。
「还有我的小的，我可怜的小的，说不定我永远抱不着他了，给他取什么名字呢？」
「腓特烈克或者弗里德里卡。」
「不；玛尔塔更好听。如果是个女孩，就用她父亲临终那一刻——」
「腓特烈，你怎么老说死？要是你回来——」
「唉！*要是！*」他叹了口气，重复道。
天将破晓时，我哭累的双眼合上了，一阵浅睡落在我们两人身上。我们交臂躺着，却始终没有失去这个意识：这是我们的诀别之刻。
我突然惊起，迸发出大声的呻吟。腓特烈立刻起身。
「看在上帝分上，玛尔塔，你怎么了？还不到时候吧？哦你说呀！是不是——」
我肯定地点了点头。
从他唇边逸出的是一声喊、一句咒诅，还是一句祷告？他抓住铃铛，发出了警报。
「马上跑去请医生——请产婆，」他向闻声赶来的女仆喊道。随即他跪倒在我身旁，吻着我垂下的手。
「我的妻！我的一切！可*如今，如今*我却得走了。」
我说不出话。人所能想象的最剧烈的身体疼痛正撕扯、绞拧着我的身体；而比这更可怕的是我灵魂的痛楚：他「*如今，如今*却得走了」；他为这个痛不欲生。

===Original===

Those who had been summoned came quickly, and at once made themselves busy about me. At the same time Frederick had to make his last preparations for the march. After he had done this: “Doctor, doctor,” he cried, seizing the physician by both hands, “you promise me, do you not, that you will bring her through? And you will telegraph to me today, and afterwards there and there,” naming the stations which he had to pass on the march. “And if there is any danger﻿—Ah! but what good is it?” he interrupted himself. “If even the danger were ever so great, could I come back then?”
“It is hard, baron,” the physician replied; “but do not be too anxious, the patient is young and strong. This evening it will be all over, and you will receive a tranquillising despatch.”
“Oh yes! You mean to send good news in any case, because the opposite would do no good! But I *will* have the truth! Listen, doctor! I must have your most sacred word of honour on it. The *whole* truth. Only on this condition could a tranquillising account really give me tranquillity. Otherwise I should think it all a lie. So swear to do this.”
The physician gave the promise required.
“O my poor, poor husband”﻿—the thought cut me to the soul﻿—“even if you receive the news today that your Martha is lying on her deathbed, you cannot turn back to close her eyes! You have something more important on hand﻿—the claims of the Augustenburgs to a throne.”
“Frederick!” I cried out loud.
He flew to my side. At this moment the clock struck. He had now only a minute or two. But we were cheated out of even this last respite, for another attack seized me, and instead of the words of adieu, I could only utter groans of anguish.
“Go, baron﻿—finish this scene,” said the physician, “for the patient such excitement is dangerous.”
One more kiss, and he rushed out. My cries and the doctor’s last word, “dangerous,” gave him his dismissal.
In what frame of mind must he have been when he departed? The local newspapers of Olmütz gave this report next day:﻿—
“Yesterday the —th Regiment left our town with music playing and banners waving, to gain fresh laurels for themselves in the sea-surrounded brotherland. Cheerful courage filled the ranks; one could see the joy of battle glowing in the men’s eyes﻿—” and so on, and so on.

===Chinese===

被请来的人迅速赶到，立刻在我身边忙碌起来。与此同时，腓特烈不得不做他行前最后的准备。做完之后：「医生，医生，」他抓住医生的双手喊道，「您答应我，您会让她挺过来的，是不是？您今天就来电报，之后到那儿、到那儿，」他一一报出他行军途中要经过的站点。「万一有什么危险——唉！可这又顶什么用？」他打断了自己。「就算危险再大，难道那时我能回来吗？」
「这很难受，男爵，」医生答道，「可您别太焦虑，病人年轻力壮。今晚一切就会过去，您会收到一封安神的电报。」
「哦是！您是横竖都打算报好消息的，因为反面的消息也无济于事！可我*就要*真话！听着，医生！我要您拿最神圣的名誉向我担保。*全部*真话。只有这样，一封安神的报告才能真正给我安神。否则我会把这一切都当作谎话。所以请您起誓照办。」
医生按要求起了誓。
「哦我可怜的、可怜的丈夫」——这个念头剜着我的心——「哪怕你今天收到消息说你的玛尔塔已躺在临终的床上，你也回不来给她合上眼睛！你手头有更要紧的事——奥古斯滕堡家的王位要求。」
「腓特烈！」我大声喊了出来。
他飞到我身边。恰在此刻，时钟响了。他只剩一两分钟了。可连这最后的喘息也被剥夺了，因为阵痛又一次攫住了我，代替道别的话语，我所能发出的只有痛苦的呻吟。
「走吧，男爵——别再演这一幕了，」医生说，「这样的激动对病人很危险。」
又一个吻，他便冲了出去。我的哭喊和医生最后那句「危险」，给他送了行。
他离去时怀着怎样的心境呢？第二天奥尔米茨的地方报纸这样报道：——
「昨日，第—团在军乐与飘扬的旗帜中开出我城，前往那四面环海的兄弟之邦为自己再添桂冠。队伍里洋溢着快活的勇气；人们眼中燃烧着求战的光芒——」云云，云云。

===Original===

Frederick had already telegraphed to Aunt Mary before his departure that I was in want of her help, and she came a few hours later to me. She found me senseless and in great danger.
For several weeks I hovered between life and death. My child died the day of its birth. The mental pain, which parting from my beloved husband had caused me, just at the time when I wanted all my strength to master the bodily pain, had rendered me incapable of bearing up against it, and I was near succumbing altogether.
The physician was obliged by his plighted word to send my poor husband the sorrowful news that the child was dead, and the mother in danger of death.
As to the news which came from him, they could not be communicated to me. I knew no one and was delirious day and night. A strange delirium. I brought back with me a feeble reminiscence of it into the period of recovered consciousness, but to reproduce this in reasonable words would be impossible for me. In the abnormal whirl of the fevered brain, conceptions and images form themselves for which there is no expression in language suitable to our normal thoughts. Only so much can I set down﻿—and I have attempted to fix the fantastic sketch in the red volumes﻿—that I confused the two events﻿—the war and my confinement﻿—together. I fancied that cannon and naked weapons (I distinctly felt the bayonet thrusts) were the instruments of delivery, and that I was lying there the prize of contention between two armies rushing on each other. That my husband had marched out I knew, but I saw him still in the form of the dead Arno, while by my side Frederick dressed as a sick nurse was stroking the silver stork. Every moment I was awaiting the bursting shell which was to shatter us all three﻿—Arno, Frederick, and me﻿—to pieces, in order that the child could come into the world, who was destined to rule over “Denstein, Schlesmark, and Holwig.”﻿ ﻿… And all this gave me such unspeakable pain and was so unnecessary.﻿ ﻿… There must, however, be someone somewhere who could change it and remove it all, who could lift off this mountain from my heart and that of all humanity by some word of power; and I was devoured with a longing to cast myself at this somebody’s feet and pray to him: “Help us! for the sake of mercy and justice help us! Lay down your arms! down!” With this cry on my lips I woke one day to consciousness.

===Chinese===

腓特烈临行前已电告玛丽姨母（Aunt Mary）说我需要她帮忙，几小时后她就来了。她发现我已不省人事，命在旦夕。
一连几个星期，我在生死之间徘徊。我的孩子出生当天就死了。与挚爱丈夫诀别所造成的精神痛苦，恰恰落在我最需要全部气力去挺住身体疼痛的当口，使我无力支撑，几乎就此沉沦。
医生碍于自己的誓言，不得不给我可怜的丈夫发去悲报：孩子死了，母亲命危。
至于从他那边来的消息，则无法告知我。我谁也不认得，日夜说着谵语。一种奇怪的谵语。苏醒之后，我从中带回一点淡薄的印象，但要用明白的话把它复述出来，对我来说是不可能的。在发热头脑的反常旋涡里，种种概念和意象自行成形，它们在我们的正常思维里找不到语言可表达。我能记下的只有这么多——我也曾试图把这幅奇幻的速写固定在红皮日记里——我把两件事——战争和我的分娩——混在了一起。我幻想大炮和赤裸的兵器（我分明感到刺刀的戳刺）是助产的器械，而我躺在那里，是两支对冲的军队争夺的战利品。丈夫已经开拔我是知道的，可我看见的仍是死去的阿尔诺的形象，而身旁穿着病号服看护装束的腓特烈正抚摸着那只银鹳鸟。我时时刻刻在等待那颗将把我们三个——阿尔诺、腓特烈和我——炸得粉碎的榴弹，好叫那个孩子得以降生，那孩子命中注定要统治「丹麦斯泰因、石勒斯马克和荷尔维克」。……而这一切给我说不出的痛苦，又全然无谓。……然而总该在什么地方有一个人，能改变这一切、解除这一切，能用一句有威力的话，从我心底、也从全人类的心底搬走这座大山；我焦灼地渴望投身到这个人的脚前恳求他：「救救我们！看在仁慈与公义的分上救救我们！放下武器！放下！」一天，我就是唇边带着这声呼喊，醒转过来的。

===Original===

My father and Aunt Mary were standing at the foot of the bed, and the former said to me to hush me:﻿—
“Yes, yes, child, be quiet. All arms down.”
This recovery of the sense of personality after a long suspension of the intellect is certainly a strange thing. First the joyful astonished discovery that one is alive, and then the anxious questioning with oneself who one really is.﻿ ﻿…
But the sudden answer to that question, which burst in with full light upon me, changed the just awakened pleasure of existence into violent pain. I was the sick Martha Tilling, whose newborn child was dead, and whose husband was gone to battle.﻿ ﻿… How long ago? That I knew not.
“Is he alive?﻿—have you letters there?﻿—messages?” were my first questions. Yes; there was quite a little heap of letters and telegrams piled up which had come during my illness. Most of them were merely inquiries after *my* condition, requests for daily, and as far as possible, hourly information. This, of course, was so long as the writer was at places where the telegraph could reach him.
I was not permitted to read Frederick’s letters at once; they thought it would excite me too much and disturb me; and now that I was hardly awake out of my delirium I must, before all things, have repose. They could tell me as much as this: “Frederick was unhurt up to the present time.” He had already been through several successful engagements. The war must now soon be over. The enemy maintained themselves at Alsen only; and if this position once were taken our troops would return, crowned with glory. This was what my father said for my comfort, and Aunt Mary gave me the history of my illness. Several weeks had now passed since her arrival, which was the very day on which Frederick departed, and my child was born and died. Of that I had preserved a recollection, but what passed in the interval﻿—my father’s arrival﻿—the news that had come from Frederick﻿—the course of my illness﻿—of all that I knew nothing. Now I heard for the first time that my condition had become so much worse that the medical men had quite given me up, and my father had been called to see me “for the last time.” The bad news must certainly have been sent to Frederick; but the better news also﻿—for the doctors had given hope again some days ago﻿—must by this time have reached him.
“If he himself is still alive,” I struck in, with a deep sigh.

===Chinese===

父亲和玛丽姨母站在床脚，前者为了安抚我说：——
「是，是，孩子，安静。武器都放下了。」
在神智长时期停摆之后重获自我，确是一件奇怪的事。先是又惊又喜地发现自己还活着，继而是惶惑地自问：我究竟是谁。……
可是那劈头照进来的、对这个问题突如其来的回答，把刚刚苏醒的生之欢愉变成了剧痛。我是病中的玛尔塔·蒂林，她新生的孩子死了，她的丈夫上了战场。……多久以前的事了？这我不知道。
「他还活着吗？——你们手上有信吗？——有电报吗？」这是我的头几个问题。有；疾病期间积攒下的信件和电报，竟堆成了小小的一堆。其中大半只是探问*我的*病情，请求每天、而且尽可能每小时报告一次。当然，这只是写信托人尚在电报能通达之处时的情形。
腓特烈的信，他们不许我立刻读；他们怕那会使我过分激动，搅扰了我；如今我才刚从谵妄中醒来，最要紧的是静养。他们可以告诉我的只有这么多：「腓特烈至今毫发无损。」他已经历了几次成功的交战。战争想必很快就要结束了。敌人只据守着阿尔森；这个阵地一旦拿下，我们的军队就会凯旋而归。这是父亲为宽慰我所说的话，玛丽姨母则给我讲了患病经过。自她到来——那正是腓特烈启程、我的孩子生下又死去的那一天——已过了好几个星期。那一段我尚存记忆；可其间的种种——父亲的到来——来自腓特烈的消息——病程——我一概不知。此刻我才头一次听说，我的病情一度恶化到医家们已全然放弃，父亲被叫来见我「最后一面」。坏消息想必一定发给了腓特烈；可好消息——几天前医生们又有了指望——此刻也必定已传到他那里了。
「只要他自己还活着，」我深深叹了一口气，插进来说。

===Original===

“Do not commit a sin, Martha,” my aunt admonished me; “the good God and His saints would not have preserved you, in answer to our prayers, in order afterwards to send such a visitation upon you. Your husband also will be preserved to you, for whom I﻿—you may believe me when I say so﻿—have prayed as fervently as for you. I have even sent him a scapulary. Oh yes! Do not shrug your shoulders; you have no trust in such things, but they can do no harm anyhow, can they? And how many proofs there are of their good effect! You yourself are again another proof what effect the intervention of the saints has; for you were, believe me, on the edge of the grave, when I addressed myself to your patron and protectress, St. Martha﻿—”
“And I,” interrupted my father, who was very clerical indeed in his politics, but in the practical way did not at all sympathise with his sister, “I wrote to Vienna for Dr. Braun, and he saved your life.”
Next day, on my urgent prayer, I was permitted to read through all the messages that had come from Frederick. Mostly they were only questions in a single line, or news equally laconic. “An engagement yesterday. I am unhurt.” “We march again today. Send messages to﻿—” A longer letter bore this direction on the envelope: “To be delivered only if all danger is over.” This I read last:﻿—

===Chinese===

「可别犯罪啊，玛尔塔，」姨母告诫我说；「仁慈的上帝和诸位圣徒既然应了我们的祈祷保全了你，就不会再把那样的灾祸降给你。你的丈夫也会保全下来还给你的，为了他我——您可以相信我这句话——我祈祷得和为您一样恳切。我甚至还给他寄去了一枚圣牌。哦是！别耸肩膀；您不信这些东西，可它们横竖没坏处，对不对？灵验的凭证又那么多！您自己就又是一桩凭证，足见圣徒代祷的效验；因为您那时候，请相信我，已经站在坟墓边上了，我便求告了您的庇护主、圣玛尔塔——」
「而我呢，」父亲打断了她。他在政治上实在非常教士气，实际做事却全然不赞同他的妹妹，「我写信到维也纳（Vienna）请来了布劳恩医生，是他救了你的命。」
第二天，经我恳切请求，他们允许我把腓特烈寄来的全部音讯读了一遍。多半只是单行的问话，或者同样简短的消息。「昨日一仗。我无恙。」「今日又开拔。音讯寄至——」有一封较长的信，信封上写着：「须待危险全部过去方可交付。」这封信我留到最后读：——

===Original===

> “My all! Will you ever read this? The last news which reached me from your physician ran: ‘Patient in high fever; condition grave.’ ‘Grave!’ He used the expression perhaps out of consideration, so as not to say ‘Hopeless.’ If you have this put into your hands you will know by that that you have escaped the danger; but you may think, in addition, what my feelings were, as, on the eve of a battle, I pictured to myself that my adored wife was lying on her deathbed; that she was calling for me, stretching out her arms for me. We did not even say any regular adieu to each other; and our child, about whom I had had such joy, dead! And tomorrow, I myself﻿—suppose a bullet find me? If I knew beforehand that you were no more, the mortal shot would be the dearest thing to me; but if you are preserved﻿—no! then I do not wish to know anything more of death. The ‘joy of dying,’ that unnatural feeling which the field preachers are always pressing on us, is one no happy man can know; and if you are alive, and I reach home, I have still untold treasures of bliss to gather. Oh, the joy of living with which we two will enjoy the future, if any such is to be our lot.
> “Today we met the enemy for the first time. Up to that our way had been through conquered territory, from which the Danes had retreated. Smoking ruins of villages, ravaged cornfields, weapons and knapsacks lying about, spots where the land was ploughed up by the shells, blood stains, bodies of horses, trenches filled with the slain﻿—such are the features of the scenes through which we have been moving in the rear of the victors, in order, if possible, to add more victories to the account﻿—i.e., to burn more villages, and so forth.﻿ ﻿… And that we have done today. We have carried the position. Behind us lies a village in flames. The inhabitants had the good luck to have quitted it beforehand; but in the stable a horse had been forgotten. I heard the beast in despair stamping and shrieking. Do you know what I did? It will procure me no decoration most certainly; for, instead of bringing down a Dane or two, I rushed to the stable to set the poor horse free. Impossible; the manger had already caught fire, then the straw under his hoofs, then his mane. So I put two revolver bullets through his head. He fell down dead, and was saved from the pain of being burned to death.

===Chinese===

> 「我的一切！你还会读到这封信吗？你医生转来的最后消息是：『病人高烧；病势危重。』『危重』！他也许是出于体贴才用这个词，好不说出『无望』。这封信若到了你手里，你便由此知道你已脱险；可你还可以再想一想，当我在一场大战前夜，想象我深爱的妻子躺在临终的床上、呼唤着我、朝我伸出双臂时，我是什么心情。我们彼此连一句正经的道别都没来得及说；而我们的孩子，我曾为之那样欢喜的孩子，死了！而明天，我自己——倘若一颗子弹找到我？假如我事先知道你已不在，那致命的一枪于我就是最亲的东西；可倘若你保全了下来——不！那我就不愿再知道死亡这回事。『求死的欢喜』，随军牧师们总向我们絮叨的那份反常的感情，是任何一个幸福的人都不会懂的；而只要你活着，我也能到家，我还有数不尽的幸福宝藏可采。哦，那我们一起去活、去享受未来的生之欢乐，倘若那样的未来归我们所有。
> 「今天我们头一回接敌。在那之前，我们一路走的是被征服的土地，丹麦人已从那里退走。冒烟的村庄废墟、被蹂躏的麦田、四处遗落的武器和背囊、被炮弹犁开的地面、血迹、马的尸体、填满了死者的堑壕——这便是我们在胜利者身后一路穿行的种种景象，为的是——倘若可能——再给这份账上添几场胜利——也就是再多烧几个村庄，等等。……而今天我们就干了这个。我们拿下了阵地。我们身后躺着一座燃烧的村庄。居民们幸而事先撤离了；可马厩里忘了一匹马。我听见那牲口绝望地刨踏嘶叫。你知道我做了什么吗？这 certainly 不会替我挣来勋章；因为我不但没有去撂倒一两个丹麦人，反而冲进马厩去救那匹可怜的马。不可能了；食槽已经着火，接着是他蹄下的稻草，接着是他的鬃毛。于是我朝他头上开了两颗左轮枪弹。他倒下死了，免去了被活活烧死的痛苦。

===Original===

Then, back into the fight, the deathly smell of the powder, the wild alarm of the whistling bullets, falling buildings, savage war-cries. Most of those around me, friends and foes, were, it is true, seized by the delirium of battle; but I remained in unblessed sobriety. I could not get myself up to hate the Danes. They are brave men, and what did they do but their duty in attacking us? My thoughts were with you, Martha! I saw you laid out on your bier, and what I wished for myself was that the bullet might strike me. But at intervals, nevertheless, a ray of longing and of hope would shine again. ‘What if she is alive? What if I should get home again?’
> “The butchery lasted more than two hours, and we remained as I said, in possession of the field. The routed enemy fled. We did not pursue. We had work enough to do on the field. A hundred paces distant from the village stood a large farmhouse, with many empty dwelling-rooms and stables; here we were to rest for the night and hither we have brought our wounded. The burial of the dead is to be done tomorrow morning. Some of the living will, of course, be shovelled in with them, for the ‘stiff cramp’ after a severe wound is a common phenomenon. Many who have remained out, whether dead or wounded, or even unwounded, we are obliged to abandon entirely, especially those who are lying under the ruins of the fallen houses. There they may, if dead, moulder slowly where they are; if wounded, bleed slowly to death; if unwounded, die slowly of famine. And we, hurrah! may go on with our jolly, joyous war!
> “The next engagement will probably be a general action. According to all appearance there will be two entire *corps d’armée* opposed to each other. The number of the killed and wounded may in that case easily rise to 10,000; for when the cannons begin their work of vomiting out death the front ranks on both sides are soon wiped out. It is certainly a wonderful contrivance. But still better would it be if the science of artillery could progress to such a point that any army could fire a shot which would smash the whole army of the enemy at one blow. Then, perhaps, all waging of war would be entirely given up. Force would then, provided the total power of the two combatants were equally great, no longer be looked to for the solution of questions of right.
> “Why am I writing all this to you?

===Chinese===

> 然后，再回到战斗里，火药那死亡的气味，呼啸的子弹那疯狂的警号，倒塌的房屋，野蛮的呐喊。我周围的大多数人，无论敌我，确实都被战斗的谵狂攫住了；可我保持着不受祝福的清醒。我没法让自己恨丹麦人。他们是勇敢的人，他们攻击我们，不过是尽他们的本分。我的心思在你身上，玛尔塔！我看见你停在灵床上，我为自己祈求的，是那颗子弹能击中我。可其间，渴望与希望的光线仍会时时重新亮起。『她要是还活着呢？我要是还能回家呢？』
> 「屠杀持续了两个多小时，而我们如我所说，据有了战场。溃败的敌人逃走了。我们没有追击。我们在战场上有的是事要做。离村庄一百步远有一座大农庄，有许多空着的住屋和厩舍；我们就在这里过夜，伤员也抬到了这里。阵亡者的掩埋定在明晨。有些活着的自然也会同他们一道被铲进土里，因为重伤之后的『僵直』是常见的现象。许多人留在了外面，死的、伤的、乃至没伤的，我们只得全然舍弃，尤其是那些压在倒塌房屋废墟底下的。他们在那里，若是死的，就慢慢朽在那里；若是伤的，就慢慢流血至死；若是没伤的，就慢慢饿死。而我们，万岁！可以继续我们这场快活欢乐的战争！
> 「下一仗多半会是一场大会战。照一切迹象看，将有整整两个*军*对垒。到那时杀伤数目很容易上到一万；因为大炮一开工呕吐死亡，双方的前列很快就扫光了。这确实是一件奇妙的发明。可要是炮兵科学能进步到这一步——随便哪支军队都能放一炮，把敌军一炮砸得全军覆没——那才更好呢。到那时，只要交战双方的总力相当，武力就再也不会被人指望用来裁决是非了。
> 「我为什么给你写这一切？

===Original===

Why do I not break out, as a warrior should, into exalted hymns of triumph over our warlike work? Why? Because I thirst after truth, and after its expression without any reserve; because at all times I hate lying phrases; but at this moment, when I am so near death myself, and am speaking to you who, perhaps, are yourself lying in the death-agony, it presses on me doubly to speak what is in my heart. Even though a thousand others should think differently, or should hold themselves bound at least to speak differently, I will, nay, I *must* say it once more before I fall a sacrifice to war﻿—I hate war. If only every man who feels the same would dare to proclaim it aloud, what a threatening protest would be shouted out to heaven! All the hurrahs which are now resounding, and all the cannon-thunder that accompanies them, would then be drowned by the battle-cry of humanity panting after humanity, by the victorious cry denouncing ‘war on war.’
> “Half-past three in the morning. I wrote the above last night. Then I lay down on a sack of straw and slept for an hour or two. We shall break up in half-an-hour, and then I shall be able to give this to the field-post. All is stirring now and getting ready for the march. Poor fellows! they have got little rest since the bloody work accomplished yesterday: little refreshment for that which is to be accomplished today. I began with a turn round our improvised field-hospital, which is to remain here. There I saw among the wounded and dying a pair for whom I would gladly have done the same as for the horse in the fire﻿—put a bullet as a coup de grâce through their heads. One was a man who had had his whole lower jaw shot away, and the other﻿—but enough. I cannot help him. Nothing can but Death. Unfortunately he is often so slow. If a man calls in despair for him he stands deaf before him. On the other hand, he is far too busy in snatching those away who with all their heart are hoping to recover, and calling on him beseechingly: ‘Oh, spare me, for I have a beloved wife pining for me at home!’ My horse is saddled, so now I must close these lines. Farewell, Martha, if you are still here!”

===Chinese===

> 我为什么不像个战士该做的那样，对我们的武功放声高唱得胜的颂歌？为什么？因为我渴求真理，渴求它毫无保留的表达；因为我一向憎恨谎言的空话；而在此刻，当我自己离死亡这么近，又是在对你——你自己也许正躺在死亡的挣扎里——说话的时候，把心里的话说出来于我是双倍要紧的事。哪怕有一千个人另作想头，或者至少自觉不得不说另一样的话，我也要——不，我*必须*——在我沦为战争的牺牲品之前再说一遍：我恨战争。但愿每一个有同感的人都敢把它高声宣告出来，那将是怎样一声直冲云霄的、威慑的抗议啊！如今回响着的所有欢呼，和为之伴奏的万炮齐鸣，都将被人类渴念人类的人性呐喊、被那声讨『向战争开战』的胜利呼号所淹没。
> 「凌晨三点半。以上是昨夜写的。随后我躺在一个草袋上睡了一两个钟头。半小时后我们就拔营，那时我就能把这封信交给军邮了。此刻一切都在动起来，整装待发。可怜的人们！昨天那场血腥的活计之后，他们没得多少休息，也没得多少补给，就要去干今天等着干的活。我先绕到我们那座将留驻此地的临时战地医院走了一圈。在伤员和垂死者中间，我看见两个人，我很乐意像对火中那匹马一样对待他们——朝他们头部补上一颗子弹，作为一种解脱。一个是整个下颚被打掉的人，另一个——罢了。我帮不了他。什么也帮不了，除了死亡。不幸的是他常常来得那么慢。人绝望地呼唤他时，他站在人面前装聋。另一方面，他又忙着把那些一心盼着痊愈、哀告着『哦，饶了我吧，家里还有爱我的妻子在苦等』的人夺走。我的马备好了鞍，此刻我必须搁笔了。永别了，玛尔塔，倘若你还在这世上！」

---
Luckily there were tidings of a later date in the packet than the letter above quoted. After the great battle predicted in the last Frederick had been able to tell me:﻿—“The day is ours. I am unhurt. These are two pieces of good news, the first for your papa, the second for you. But I cannot overlook the fact that the same day has brought numberless griefs to numberless others.﻿ ﻿…”
In another letter Frederick related how he had met with his cousin Godfrey.

===Chinese===

---
所幸这一包音讯里，还有比上面所引那封更晚的消息。在那封信里预言的大会战之后，腓特烈已得便告诉我：——「这一天是我们的了。我无恙。这是两条好消息，第一条给你爸爸，第二条给你。可我无法回避：同一天，它也给数不清的旁人带去了数不清的悲恸。……」
在另一封信里，腓特烈讲述了遇见他表弟戈特弗里德的事。

===Original===

> “Picture to yourself my astonishment. Whom should I see riding before me at the head of a detachment, but Aunt Cornelia’s only son! How the poor woman must be trembling for him.﻿ ﻿… The young man himself is all eagerness and love of battle. I saw it in his proud, joyful bearing, and he has also told me so. We were in camp together the same evening and I invited him into my tent. ‘It is indeed splendid,’ he cried out in rapture, ‘that we are fighting in the same cause, cousin, and together. Am not I in luck, that war should have broken out in the first year of my lieutenancy? I shall gain the Cross of Merit.’ ‘And my aunt, how did she take your departure?’ ‘Oh! in the mother’s way, with tears﻿—which she did all she could to hide, so as not to damp my spirit﻿—with blessings, with grief, and with pride.’ ‘And what were your feelings when you first got into the melée?’ ‘Oh, delightful! ennobling!’ ‘You need not use falsehood to me, my dear boy. It is not the staff officer who is asking about your feelings as a lieutenant bound to duty, but a man and a friend.’ ‘I can only repeat, delightful and ennobling. Awful, I grant, but so magnificent. And the consciousness that I am fulfilling, with God’s help, the highest duty of a man to king and country! And further, that I see Death, the spectre elsewhere so feared and shunned, so close and busy all round me, his very breath breathing over me﻿—the thought raises me to a mood of mind so elevated above the common, so epic that I feel the muse of history hovering over our heads and lending our swords the might of victory. A noble rage glows in me against the presumptuous foe, who would have trampled on the rights of the German countries, and it is to me an enthusiasm to have the power of gratifying this hatred. It is a curious, mysterious thing, this power of killing﻿—nay, this compulsion to kill﻿—without being a murderer﻿—with a fearless exposure of one’s own life.’
> “So the boy chattered on. I let him talk. I had similar feelings when my first battle was raging round me. ‘Epic!’﻿—yes, there you hit on the right word. The heroic poems and the heroic histories by whose means our schools bring us up to be warriors, these are what are set vibrating in our brains by the thunders of the cannonade, the flash of naked weapons, and the shouts of the combatants.

===Chinese===

> 「你想象一下我的惊讶。走在一支分队前头迎面而来的，不是别人，正是科内莉娅姨母的独子！那可怜的母亲此刻该怎样为他提心吊胆。……这年轻人自己却满腔是求战的热情。这从他那骄傲、快活的神气里看得出来，他也亲口对我说了。当晚我们在同一个营地宿营，我请他到我的帐篷里来。『我们竟为同一桩事业并肩作战，表哥，真是太美了，』他狂喜地喊道，『我多走运，战争偏偏在我任少尉的头一年爆发！我要挣得功勋章。』『姨母呢，她怎么送你走的？』『哦！按母亲的方式，流着泪——又百般遮掩，免得挫了我的锐气——祝福着，悲伤着，也骄傲着。』『你头一回杀进混战时是什么心情？』『哦，痛快！使人高尚！』『跟我就不必说假话了，亲爱的孩子。现在问你的不是要核查部下心境的参谋军官，是一个人和一个朋友。』『我只能再说一遍：痛快，高尚。可怕，我承认，可又那么壮丽。还有这意识——我正在上帝的帮助下，履行一个人对君王和祖国的最高义务！再有，我看见死亡——那个在别处人人畏惧躲避的幽灵——在我四周这么近、这么忙碌，他的呼吸正吹在我脸上——这念头把我抬到一种如此超乎寻常、如此史诗的心境，我感到历史的女神正盘旋在我们头顶，把胜利的神力借给我们的剑。我胸中燃着对那狂妄之敌的高贵的义愤，他竟敢践踏德意志邦国的权利，而能有力量满足这份仇恨，于我就是一阵狂喜。杀人的这个力——不，杀人的这个强制——却不必做凶手，还要豁出自己的性命，这真是一桩奇怪而神秘的事。』
> 「这孩子就这样滔滔不绝。我由他说。我头一回打仗、战斗在四周轰鸣时，也有过相似的感情。『史诗的！』——不错，你正好说中了那个词。我们的学校用来把我们养育成军人的那些英雄史诗和英雄史传，正是它们，被炮声、兵刃的寒光和交战者的呐喊在我们脑中震响起来。

===Original===

And the freedom from ordinary circumstances, the inexplicable freedom from law in which one finds oneself all of a sudden, makes one feel as if transported into another world﻿—it is like an outlook beyond this trumpery earthly existence, with its peaceful domestic quiet, into a titanic struggle of infernal spirits. But this giddiness soon passed over with me, and it is only with an effort that I can bring back to my mind the sensations which young Tessow sketched to me. I recognised too soon that the desire for battle was not a *super*-human but an *infra*-human feeling, no mystic revelation from the realms of the morning, but a reminiscence of the realm of the animal, a reawakening of the brutal. And a man who can intoxicate himself into a savage lust for blood, who﻿—as I have seen several of our men do﻿—can cut down with uplifted sabre an unarmed enemy, who can sink into a Berserker, or lower still, a bloodthirsty tiger﻿—that is the man who, for the moment, revels in the ‘joy of battle.’ I never did this. Believe me, my wife; I never did.
> “Godfrey is delighted that we Austrians are united in fighting for the ‘right cause’ (how does he know that? As if every cause is not always represented as the ‘right’ one by its own side!) with the Prussians: ‘Yes, we Germans are all one united people of brothers!’ ‘That was seen long ago in the Thirty Years’ War, and also in the Seven Years’ War,’ I struck in half-aloud. Godfrey missed what I said, and went on: ‘For each other and with each other we can conquer every foe.’ ‘What will you say then, my young friend, if today or tomorrow the Prussians and Austrians quarrel, and we two shall be ranged as foes, one against each other?’ ‘Not conceivable, now, after the blood of both of us has flowed for the same cause. Now surely we can never more﻿—’ ‘Never more? I would warn you not to use the expressions “never” or “forever” in political matters. What ephemerides are in the scale of living beings, such are the friendships and enmities of nations in the scale of historical phenomena.’
> “I write all this down, Martha, not that I think it can interest you, poor sufferer, nor because I want to make reflections to you upon it, but I have an idea that I shall fall, and in that case I do not wish my sentiments to sink into the grave with me unuttered. My letter may even be found and read by others, if not by you.

> 而那种摆脱日常境况、一下子置身于法度之外的莫名自由，又使人恍如被搬进了另一个世界——仿佛从这寒伧的尘世生存、这安 domestic 的家常宁静里探头外望，望进一场巨灵与地狱群魔的搏斗。可这阵眩晕在我身上很快就过去了，如今要我重唤起小特索向我描述的那些感觉，还得费一把劲。我太早就认清了：好战之心不是*超*人的感情，而是*亚*人的感情，不是来自黎明之境的神秘启示，而是兽性的国度的回忆，是残忍者的复醒。而一个能把自己灌醉、灌出嗜血狂来的人——一个能像我见我们几个弟兄干过的那样，高举马刀砍杀手无寸铁之敌的人，一个能沉沦为狂战士、乃至更低下、沦为噬血之虎的人——那才是 momentarily 沉醉于『战斗之乐』的人。我从不曾这样。相信我，我的妻；我从不曾。
