Perhaps even the whip hanging up on the wall would be enough for this purpose; but if that arrogant fellow should try any of his saucy tricks he had received fair warning that it would come down upon him in the shape of the *Revanche de Sadowa*.
We, of course, decisively put aside all such consolations. A former misfortune was not to be conjured away by a fresh misfortune, nor an old injustice to be atoned for by a new injustice. We assured our friends that we wished for nothing, except that we might never see the present peace broken again. This was also essentially the wish of Napoleon III. We had so much intercourse with persons whose position was quite close to the emperor, that we had plenty of opportunities of becoming acquainted with his political views, as he gave utterance to them in his confidential conversation. It was not only that he wished for peace at the moment﻿—he cherished the plan of proposing to the powers a general disarmament. But, for the moment, he did not feel his own domestic position in the country secure enough to carry this plan out. There was great discontent boiling and seething among the populace; and in the circle immediately surrounding the throne there was a party which laboured to represent to him that his throne could only be rendered secure by a successful foreign war﻿—just a little triumphal promenade to the Rhine, and the splendour and stability of the Napoleonic dynasty were secured. *Il faut faire grand*, was the advice of his counsellors. That the war, which was in prospect the year before on the Luxembourg question, had come to nothing, and was displeasing to them; the preparations on both sides had gone on so grandly, and then the matter had been adjourned. But in the long run a fight between France and Prussia was certainly inevitable. They were incessantly urging on further in this direction. But only a feeble echo of these matters came to us. One is accustomed to hear that sort of thing resounding in the journals, as regularly as the breakers on the shore. There is no occasion to fear a storm on that account. You listen quite tranquilly to the band which is playing its lively airs on the beach﻿—the breakers form only a soft unheeded bass accompaniment to them.
This brilliant way of life, only too overburdened with pleasure, reached its highest pitch in the spring months.

也许墙上挂着的那条马鞭，为这个用途也就尽够了；不过那骄横的家伙倘若再耍什么放肆的花样，他已得到明白的警告：到时落下来的，便是「萨多瓦复仇」这形态的鞭子。
我们呢，自然断然撇开这一切安慰。旧的不幸不能靠新的不幸来禳除，旧的不公也不能靠新的不公来抵偿。我们向朋友们保证，我们别无所愿，只愿再别看见眼前的和平被打破。这也基本上是拿破仑三世的心愿。我们同地位极近皇帝的人交往甚多，有的是机会熟悉他的政见——他在密谈里流露出来的政见。他不仅眼前盼望和平——他还怀着一个向列强提议普遍裁军的计划。只是眼下他还不觉得自己在国内的根基稳固到足以推行这个计划。民众中间沸沸扬扬，酝酿着巨大的不满；紧围着宝座的圈子里，有一派人力图让他相信：他的宝座只有靠一场成功的外战才能坐稳——只消到莱茵河畔做一次小小的凯旋散步，拿破仑王朝的光辉与稳固便都有了保障。*Il faut faire grand*——要干就干大的：他的谋臣这样进言。去年卢森堡问题上眼看要打的那一仗竟没打成，很叫他们不痛快；两边的备战办得那样轰轰烈烈，到头来事情却延期了。可长远看，法国同普鲁士的一仗终归免不了。他们一刻不停地朝这个方向赶。这些事情传到我们耳里的，不过是微弱的回声。人听惯了报章里这一类声响，就像听惯岸边的碎浪一样。不必因此担心起风暴。你只管安安静静听着乐队在沙滩上奏它轻快的曲子——碎浪不过是给它们伴一段轻柔的、无人留意的低音。
这种被欢娱压得过重、却光彩夺目的生活，到春季几个月达到了顶峰。

At that time there were added long drives in the Bois in open carriages, numerous picture exhibitions, garden parties, horse-races, picnics, and with all this no fewer theatres, or visits, or dinner or evening parties, than in the depth of winter. We then began to long much for repose. In fact, this sort of life has never its true attraction, except when some flirtation or love affair is combined with it. Girls who are in search of a husband, women who want a lover, or men who are in search of adventures, for these every new fête, where it is possible they may meet the object of their dream, possesses a new interest, but for Frederick and me? That I was inflexibly true to my lord, that I never by a single glance gave anyone the occasion to approach me with any audacious hopes, I may say, without any pride of virtue﻿—it was a mere matter of course. Whether, under different relations, I should also have resisted all the temptations to which, in such a whirl of pleasure, pretty young ladies are exposed, is more than I can say; but when one carries in one’s heart a love so deep and so full of bliss as I felt for my Frederick, one is surely armed against all danger. And as far as he was concerned, was he true to me? I can only say, that I never felt any doubt about it.
When the summer had returned to the land, when the Grand Prix was over, and the different members of society began to quit Paris, some to Trouville or Dieppe, Biarritz or Vichy, others to Baden Baden, and a third set to their châteaux, Princess Mathilde to St. Gratien, and the court to Compiègne, then we were besieged with requests to select the same destinations for travel, and with invitations to country-houses; but we were decidedly indisposed to prolong the campaign of luxury and pleasure which we had carried out in the winter, into a summer one also. I did not wish to return at once to Grumitz. I feared too much the reawakening of painful memories; besides, we should not have found there the solitude we desired, on account of our numerous relations and neighbours. So we chose once more for our resting-place a quiet corner of Switzerland. We promised our friends in Paris that we would come back next winter, and went on our summer tour with the joy of schoolboys going for their holidays.
Now succeeded a time of real refreshment.

===Chinese===

那时节又添上乘敞篷马车在布洛涅林苑里长驱兜风，无数的画展、游园会、赛马、野宴，而与此同时，看戏、拜客、晚宴和夜会，一点也不比隆冬时节少。我们于是开始切切盼望休憩。说实在的，这种生活除非配上几分调情或情事，否则从没有它真正的吸引力。待嫁的姑娘、想要情人的妇人、寻艳遇的男人——对他们，每一场新的欢会都可能遇见梦中之物，自有新趣味；可对腓特烈和我呢？至于我对夫君坚贞不渝、从不曾用一个眼色给过任何人胆敢存非分之想的由头——这话我可以说，毫无德色——那不过是理所当然。倘若境遇不同，换了我，能否抵得住漂亮少妇们在这样的欢娱旋涡里所受的一切诱惑，那就非我所知了；可当人心里装着一段像我对我腓特烈这样深、这样圆满的爱情时，人是武装齐全、不惧一切危险的。至于他，他忠实于我吗？我只能说，我从不曾对此有过一丝怀疑。
夏天回到大地，大赛马结束，社交界的人士开始各奔东西：有的去特鲁维尔或多维尔、比亚里茨或维希，有的去巴登-巴登，第三拨回各自的城堡，玛蒂尔德公主去圣格拉蒂安，宫廷去贡比涅。于是我们也被人缠住，劝我们选同样的去处，请我们到乡间别墅做客；可我们决计不愿把我们冬天打的那场奢侈与欢娱的战役，再延长成一场夏季战役。我又不愿立刻回格鲁米茨。我怕唤醒痛苦的回忆；何况那里有我们众多的亲戚邻里，我们找不到想要的清静。于是我们再选了瑞士一个安静的角落作休憩地。我们向巴黎的朋友们许诺冬天再来，然后怀着学童放假般的欢喜，踏上了夏日的旅程。
接着来的是一段真正焕发精神的时光。

===Original===

Long walks, long hours of study, long hours of play with the children, and no entries in the red volumes﻿—which last was a sign of freedom from care, and spiritual peace.
Europe also seemed at that time tolerably free from care, and peaceful. At least no “black spots” were anywhere visible. One did not even hear any more talk about the famous *Revanche de Sadowa*. The greatest trouble which I experienced at that time was caused by the universal obligation for defence which had been introduced a year before amongst us Austrians. That my Rudolf some time or other *must* become a soldier﻿—that was a thing I could not bear. And yet folks dream of freedom!
Frederick tried to comfort me. “A year of ‘volunteering’ is not much.” I shook my head.
“Even if it were but a day! No man ought to be compelled to take upon himself a certain office, which perhaps he hates, even for a single day; for during that day he must make a show of the opposite of what he feels﻿—must pretend that he is doing joyfully what he really hates﻿—in short, he is obliged to lie, and I wanted to bring up my son to be true, before all things.”
“Then he ought to have been born one or two centuries later, my dearest,” replied Frederick. “It is only the perfectly free man who can be perfectly true; and we are still poorly off for both things﻿—freedom and truth﻿—in our days; that becomes clearer and clearer to me the deeper I plunge into my studies.”
Now, in this retirement Frederick had twice the leisure for his work, and he set about it with true ardour. However happy and content we were with our life in this solitude, still we remained firm in our determination to spend next winter in Paris again. This time, however, it was not with the view of amusing ourselves, but in order to do something practical towards the fulfilment of the task of our lives. In this, it is true, we did not cherish any *confidence* that we should attain anything; but when a man sees even the possibility of the shadow of a chance offered him to contribute anything towards a cause which he recognises as the holiest cause on earth, he feels it to be a duty which he cannot refuse, to try this chance.

===Chinese===

长长的散步，长长的研读，同孩子们长长的游玩，红皮日记本里则一笔不记——这末一条，正是无忧无虑、心境平和的表征。
那时的欧洲，看来也相当无忧，相当太平。至少「黑点」哪儿也看不见了。连那著名的「萨多瓦复仇」，人们也不大再谈起了。我那时遭到的最大的烦恼，来自一年前我们奥地利人中间推行的普遍防御义务。想到我的鲁道夫迟早*必须*当兵——这是我不能忍受的事。可人们还梦想自由呢！
腓特烈试着安慰我。「一年『志愿兵』不算什么。」我摇头。
「哪怕只有一天也不行！任何人都不该被迫去承担一种他也许厌恶的职分，哪怕只承担一天；因为在那一天里，他必须装出与他所感相反的样子——必须假装欢欢喜喜地做他心里厌恶的事——总而言之，他不得不说谎；而我首要的，是想把我的儿子教养成为一个真实的人。」
「那他该晚一两百年出生才对，我最亲爱的，」腓特烈答道，「唯有完全自由的人才能完全真实；而这两样东西——自由与真实——在我们这时代都还贫乏得很；我钻研得越深，这一点看得越清楚。」
在这隐居中，腓特烈做工的余闲多了一倍，他以真正的热忱着手干了起来。我们虽然在孤独中过得幸福而满足，却仍拿定主意，下一个冬天再去巴黎。只是这一回，不是为了寻欢，而是要为我们毕生的任务做点切实的事。诚然，我们并不*指望*能成就什么；可是，当一个人看见一线机会的影子的可能性，容他为一件他认作世上最神圣的事业尽一分力，他便觉得试一试这机会，是一份推卸不掉的义务。

===Original===

Now, in recapitulating, during our familiar talks, the recollections of Paris, we had thought also of that plan of the Emperor Napoleon which had come to our ears by the communications of his confidants﻿—I mean the plan for proposing disarmament to the great powers. It was on this that we based our hopes and our projects. Frederick’s researches had brought into his hand Sully’s *Memoirs*, in which the plan of Henry IV for peace is described in all its details. We meant to convey an abstract of this to the Emperor of the French; and at the same time to try, through our connections in Austria and Prussia, to prepare both these Governments for the propositions of the French Government. I could set this on foot by the means of Minister To-be-sure, and Frederick had at Berlin a relative who was in an influential political position, and stood very well at court.
In December, which was the time we meant to move to Paris, we were prevented. Our treasure, our little Sylvia, fell ill. What anxious hours those were! Napoleon III and Henry IV of course were then put in the background﻿—our child dying!
But she did not die. In two weeks all danger was over. Only the physician forbade us to travel during the worst of the winter’s cold. So we put off our departure till March.
This sickness and recovery, the danger and the preservation﻿—what a shock they had given our hearts! and how much﻿—though I thought that no longer possible﻿—they had brought them more near to each other still! To tremble in unison before a horrid disaster﻿—one which each fears the more from seeing the other’s despair, and to weep tears of joy in common when this disaster has been averted﻿—are things which have a most mighty influence in welding souls together.
---
Forebodings? No, there were none. If there had been Paris would not have made on me the cheerful impression of promised pleasure which it did on one sunny afternoon of March, 1870, on our arrival. One knows now what horrors were brooding over that city after a very short interval; but not the faintest anticipation of trouble arose in my mind.
We had already hired beforehand, through the agent, John Arthur, the same little palace in which we had lived last year, and at its door was waiting for us our maître d’hôtel of the previous year.

===Chinese===

如今，在我们促膝闲谈、重温巴黎旧忆时，也想起了从皇帝心腹们的传闻里听来的那个拿破仑皇帝的计划——我指的是向列强提议裁军的那个计划。我们的希望与谋划便系于此。腓特烈的钻研把苏利的《回忆录》送到了他手里，亨利四世的和平计划在其中描写得巨细无遗。我们打算把它的摘要呈给法国皇帝；同时试着借我们在奥地利和普鲁士的关系，使两国政府先对法国政府的提议有所准备。这件事我可以借「诚然」大臣之力发动，腓特烈则在柏林有一位亲戚，位居政治上有影响的要职，在宫廷里又很得宠。
十二月，本是我们打算动身去巴黎的时候，我们却被绊住了。我们的宝贝、我们的小西尔维娅病了。那是些怎样的焦灼时刻啊！拿破仑三世和亨利四世自然都被抛到了脑后——我们的孩子在垂危！
可她没有死。两个星期，危险全部过去。只是医生不许我们在隆冬最冷的时候上路。于是我们把行期推到了三月。
这一场病与痊愈、这危险与保全——给了我们的心怎样的震动！而它们——尽管我以为再不可能——又把两颗心拉得多么更近！在一场可怖的灾祸面前一同战栗——各自因看见对方的绝望而愈加恐惧；灾祸解除时又一同流下喜悦的眼泪——这些事，在熔铸灵魂于一处上，有着极强大的力量。
---
预感？不，没有预感。倘若有，巴黎就不可能在1870年三月一个晴朗的午后、在我们抵达之时，还给我那般许诺着欢乐的愉快印象了。如今人人知道，短短时日之后，怎样的恐怖在这座城上空孵育；可当时我心中不曾升起一丝最微弱的不祥之感。
我们已提前经中人约翰·阿瑟租下了去年住过的那座小公馆，门口等着我们的，是去年的那位司膳总管。

===Original===

As we drove across the Champs Élysées to reach our dwelling, it was just the hour for the Bois, and several of our old acquaintances met us and exchanged joyful recognitions. The numerous little barrows of violets which were dragged about the streets of Paris that year filled the air with the promise of spring; the sunbeams were sparkling and playing in rainbows on the fountains of the *Rond-point*, making little reflections on the carriage lamps and the harness of the many carriages. Amongst others, the beautiful empress was driving in a carriage harnessed *à la Daumont*. She passed us, and, recognising me, made a gesture of salutation.
There are some special pictures or scenes which photograph or phonograph themselves on our memory, along with the feelings that accompany them, and some of the words that are spoken at them. “This Paris is truly lovely,” cried Frederick at this point, and my feeling was a childish self-congratulation at the coming treat. Had I known what was coming to me, and to this whole city, now bathed in splendour and rejoicing!
This time we abstained from throwing ourselves, as we had done the year before, into the whirlpool of worldly amusements. We announced that we would not accept any dancing invitations, and kept ourselves apart from the great receptions. Even the theatre we did not visit so often﻿—only when some piece made a great impression﻿—and so it came about that we spent most evenings at home alone, or in the society of a few friends.
As to our plans with regard to the idea of the emperor about disarmament, we got on but badly with them. Napoleon III had not, indeed, given up his idea altogether, but the present time, it was said, was not at all suited for carrying it out. In the circle around the throne a conviction had grown up that that throne stood on no very firm footing﻿—a great discontent was boiling and seething among the people, in order to repress which all the police and censorship regulations were made more stringent, and the only consequence of this was greater discontent. The only thing, said certain people, which could give renewed splendour and security to the dynasty would be a successful campaign.

===Chinese===

我们乘车穿过香榭丽舍大街回寓所，正是去布洛涅林苑的时辰，好几位旧相识迎面遇见，欢喜地互道寒温。那年巴黎街头拖来拖去数不清的紫罗兰小推车，把春天的许诺灌满空中；阳光在*圆形广场*的喷泉上闪出七彩，映在许多马车的车灯与马具上，碎光点点。其中，美丽的皇后乘着一辆*多蒙式*驾套的马车驶过。她与我们交臂而过，认出了我，做了一个致意的手势。
有些特别的画面或场景，会连同伴随它们的情感、连同当时说的几句话，照相或留声一般印在记忆里。「这巴黎真是可爱，」腓特烈这时喊道；而我的心情，是对即将到来的欢娱一种孩子气的自喜。倘若我知道等着我的、等着这座正沐浴在繁华与欢腾中的城市的是什么！
这一回，我们不再像去年那样把自己抛进世俗欢娱的旋涡。我们宣布不赴任何舞会的邀请，同大型招待会也保持了距离。连戏院也不常去了——只在某出戏轰动的时候——于是我们多数夜晚独自在家度过，或同三五朋友一起。
至于我们围绕皇帝裁军构想拟的那些计划，进行得很不顺利。拿破仑三世固然没有全然放弃他的想法，但据说眼下完全不宜施行。围着宝座的那个圈子里生出了一种确信：宝座的根基不很牢——民间正沸沸扬扬酝酿着巨大的不满；为压制它，一切警察与书报检查的条例都收紧了，而唯一的结果是更大的不满。某些人说，唯一能给王朝重添光辉与稳固的，是一场成功的战局。

===Original===

It is true there was no near prospect of this, but all mention of disarmament would be a total and complete mistake, for thereby the whole Bonaparte-nimbus would be destroyed, which was undoubtedly founded on the heritage of glory of the first Napoleon. We had also received no very cheering answers to our inquiries on these subjects from Prussia and Austria. There people had entered on an epoch of expansion of the “defensive forces” (the word “army” began to be unfashionable), and the word “disarmament” fell on this like a gross discord. On the contrary, in order to obtain the blessings of peace, the “defensive power” must be increased﻿—the French were not to be trusted﻿—the Russians neither﻿—and the Italians, most certainly not﻿—they would fall on Trieste and Trent at once, if they had the opportunity﻿—in short, the only thing to do was to nurse the *Landwehr* system with all the care possible.
“The time is not ripe,” said Frederick, on our receiving communications such as these, “and I must, I suppose, in reason give up the hope that I personally may be able to help in hastening the ripening of that time, or even see the fruits I long for blossoming. What I can contribute is mean enough. But from the hour that I saw that this thing, however mean, is my duty, it has in spite of all become the greatest thing of all to me, so I keep on.”
But if for the present the project of disarmament had been dropped, I had yet one comfort﻿—there was no war in sight. The war party which existed in the court and among the people, and whose opinion was that the dynasty must be “rebaptised in blood,” and that another little taste of glory must be provided for the people, were obliged to renounce their plan of attack and their bewitching “little campaign on the Rhine frontier.” For France possessed no allies; great drought prevailed in the country; a dearth of forage was to be anticipated; the army horses had to be sold; there was no “question” in agitation; the contingent of recruits had been diminished by the legislative body; in short, so Ollivier declared from the tribune﻿—“the peace of Europe is assured.”
*Assured!* I rejoiced over the word. It was repeated in all the papers, and many thousands rejoiced with me. For what can there be better for the majority of men than assured peace?

===Chinese===

诚然，这事眼下并无近景；可是一切关于裁军的提法，都将是十足的、彻底的错误，因为整个波拿巴的光环会由此毁掉——那光环无疑建立在第一拿破仑的荣耀遗产之上。我们就这些问题向普鲁士和奥地利探问，得到的回答也不很令人振奋。那边的人已进入一个扩充「防御力量」的时代（「军队」一词开始不时兴了），「裁军」这个词落在上面，就像一个刺耳的走调音。相反，为求得和平的福佑，「防御力量」必须增强——法国人信不过——俄国人也信不过——意大利人就更不必说了——一有机会他们立刻会扑向的里雅斯特和特伦托——总而言之，唯一的办法，是竭尽一切心力把*后备军*制度抚养周到。
「时机未熟，」接到这类来信时腓特烈说，「而我，想来也只好按理放弃这份希望：指望我本人能助这时机早熟，或哪怕亲眼看见我渴念的果实开花。我能贡献的，微薄得很。可从我看清这件事——尽管微薄——是我的义务的那个钟点起，它不顾一切，终究成了我心中至大的事，所以我不停地做。」

===Original===

How much, however, that security which was announced by a statesman on June 3, 1870, was worth we now all know. And even at the time we might have known this much, that assurances of that kind from statesmen, though the public always receives them again with the same innocent trust, really contain no guarantee﻿—literally none. The European situation shows no question in agitation﻿—therefore peace is secure. What feeble logic! Questions may come into agitation any moment; it is not till we have prepared some means against such a contingency other than war, that we can ever be secure against war.

===Chinese===

然而，裁军的计划虽已搁下，我却还有一桩安慰——放眼不见战争。宫廷里与民众中的那个主战派——他们主张王朝必须「在血里重受洗礼」，主张再给人民来一小口荣耀的甜头——也不得不放弃他们的进攻计划和他们那迷人的「莱茵边境小小战役」。因为法国没有盟邦；全国大旱；草料短缺可以预见；军马不得不卖掉；没有任何一桩「问题」在酝酿；新兵配额被立法机构削减了；总而言之，奥利维耶在讲坛上宣告——「欧洲的和平是笃定的。」
*笃定！*我为这个词欢喜。所有的报纸都重复它，千千万万人同我一道欢喜。因为对大多数人来说，还有什么比笃定的和平更好呢？
然而，1870年6月3日由一位政治家宣告的这份笃定，如今我们都知道值几个钱了。而且当时我们本也可以知道这一层：政客们的这类保证，尽管公众总是一回又一回怀着同样天真的信任去领受，其实不包含任何担保——字面意义上的毫无担保。欧洲局势眼下没有问题在酝酿——所以和平是稳的。何等孱弱的逻辑！问题随时可能开始酝酿；只有当我们为这种不测备下了战争之外的其他办法，我们才能永远免于战争的威胁。

## XVII / 十七
===Original===

We Remain in Paris to Get Ready a New House﻿—The “Question” Between France and Prussia﻿—Candidature of Prince Hohenzollern for the Crown of Spain﻿—The War Rumours and the Speeches in the Chamber Become Menacing﻿—The Hohenzollern Candidature Withdrawn﻿—Further Demands of France﻿—Threatening Debate in the French Chamber﻿—War Declared﻿—Excitement and Enthusiasm in Paris﻿—with Which Side Should We Sympathise?﻿—The Opposing Manifestoes﻿—We Linger in Paris﻿—Opinions About War of Eminent French Writers﻿—Proclamations of the Two Armies﻿—Secret History.
Paris society again dispersed in all directions. We, however, remained behind on business. For an extraordinarily advantageous bargain had been offered to us. Through the sudden departure of an American a little, half-finished hotel, in the Avenue de l’Imperatrice, had had to be offered for sale, and at a price which did not amount to much more than the sum already expended on the decoration and furnishing of the thing itself. As we had already the intention of spending in future some months of each year in Paris, and as the purchase in question was also at the same time an excellent bargain, we closed with it. We wished to superintend the completion ourselves, and for this purpose stopped in Paris. The decoration of one’s own nest is, besides, such a pleasurable task that we willingly endured the unpleasantness of staying in a city the whole summer. Besides, we had plenty of houses to which we could resort for company. The château of Princess Mathilde, St. Gratien, then Château Mouchy, and next Baron Rothschild’s place, Ferrières, and other summer residences besides of our acquaintance, were situated near Paris, and we arranged once or twice a week to pay a visit, now to one of them, now to another.
It was, I recollect, in the salon of Princess Mathilde that I first heard of “the question” that was soon to come into “agitation.”
The company was sitting, after *déjeûner*, on the terrace, looking on to the park. Who were all the people there? I do not recollect them all now; only two of the persons present remain in my memory, Taine and Renan. The conversation was a very lively one, and I recollect that it was Renan chiefly who led the talk, sparkling with esprit and witticisms. The author of the *Vie de Jésus* is an example that a man may be incredibly ugly and yet exercise an incredible fascination.

===Chinese===

我们留巴黎筹备新居——法普之间的「问题」——霍亨索伦亲王候选西班牙王位——战争风声与议院演说渐趋凶险——霍亨索伦候选撤回——法国进一步的要求——法国议院的威吓性辩论——宣战——巴黎的激动与狂热——我们该同情哪一边？——针锋相对的宣言——我们滞留巴黎——法国名作家们的战争观——两军的告示——秘史。
巴黎的社交界又四散而去。我们却因事务留了下来。因为有一桩格外合算的买卖送上门来。一位美国人突然离境，皇后大道上一座半完工的小公馆不得不出售，价钱比已经花在它本身的装潢和家具上的款项多不了多少。我们本就有意今后每年在巴黎住上几个月，这桩买卖又是绝好的便宜，我们便成交了。我们想亲自督工收尾，为此留在了巴黎。何况，装点自己的巢是一件如此快意的差事，我们甘愿忍受整个夏天滞留城中的不自在。再说，可以走动做客的宅子也多的是。玛蒂尔德公主的圣格拉蒂安城堡、穆希城堡，还有罗特希尔德男爵的费里埃尔庄园，以及相识者们的其他几处消夏宅邸，都在巴黎近郊；我们约定每星期一两次，轮流到其中一家去做客。
我记得，正是在玛蒂尔德公主的沙龙里，我头一回听人说起那桩不久就要「闹起来」的「问题」。
早宴之后，一伙人坐在露台上，面向园林。在座都是些什么人？如今我已记不全了；只记得两位，泰纳和勒南。谈话极活跃，记得领谈的主要是勒南，妙语和机智火花四溅。这位《耶稣传》的作者是一个例证：人可以丑得叫人难以置信，却又魅力大得叫人难以置信。

===Original===

Now the talk turned upon politics. A candidate had been sought for the crown of Spain. A prince of Hohenzollern was to receive the crown. I had scarcely been listening, for what could the throne of Spain or he who was to sit upon it have to do with me or all these nonchalant folks here? But then someone said:﻿—
“A Hohenzollern? France would not permit that!”
The words cut me to the heart, for what did that “not permit” imply? When such an utterance comes from any country one sees with one’s mind’s eye the statue personifying that country as a gigantic virgin, her head thrown back in defiance, her hand on her sword.
The conversation, however, soon turned to another subject. How full of tremendous results this question of the Spanish throne would be none of us yet suspected. I, of course, did not either. Only, that arrogant “France would not permit that” stuck in my memory like a discord, and along with it the whole scenery did so in which it was spoken.
From that time the question of the Spanish throne became constantly more loud and more pressing. Every day the space became larger which it occupied in the newspapers and in conversations in the salons, and I know that it bored me in the highest degree, this Hohenzollern candidature: soon there was nothing else spoken of. And it was spoken of in an offended tone, as if nothing more insulting to France could take place. Most people saw behind it a provocation to war on the part of Prussia. But it was clear, so it was said, that “France could not permit such a thing, so, if the Hohenzollerns persist in it, that is a simple challenge.” I could not understand that; but in other respects I was free from anxiety. We received letters from Berlin, telling us from a well-instructed quarter that not the slightest importance was attached at court to the succession of a Hohenzollern to the Spanish crown. And, therefore, we were much more occupied with the work at our house than with politics.
But gradually we became more attentive to the subject for all that. As, before the storm, a certain rustling of leaves goes through the forest, so, before war, a rustle of certain voices goes through the world. “*Nous aurons la guerre﻿—nous aurons la guerre*,” was what resounded in the air of Paris. Then an unspeakable anxiety possessed me. Not for my own people﻿—for we, as Austrians, were at first out of the game.

===Chinese===

话题转到了政治上。西班牙的王冠正在寻找主人，一位霍亨索伦家的亲王将得到它。我先前几乎没有听，因为西班牙的王位也好，坐上去的人也好，同我、同这里这一群懒洋洋的人有什么相干？可这时有人说道：——
「霍亨索伦家的人？法兰西决不答应！」
这话刺进了我的心，因为那「决不答应」意味着什么？每当这种话从哪一个国家嘴里说出来，人就会在心里看见那国家的化身：一尊巨大的处女像，头傲然后仰，手按在剑上。
不过谈话很快就转到别的题目上去了。这西班牙王位问题将结出怎样可怕的后果，当时我们谁也没有疑心。我自然也没有。只是那句倨傲的「法兰西决不答应」，像一个走调的音，粘在了我的记忆里；连同说这话时的整个场景，也一齐粘住了。
从那时起，西班牙王位问题叫得一天比一天响，一天比一天紧。它在报纸上、在沙龙谈话里占的地盘天天见大；我知道，这桩霍亨索伦候选的公案让我烦透了：不久，别的话题就没有了。而且人们谈起它用的是一种受了冒犯的口气，仿佛再没有比这更侮辱法兰西的事了。多数人从背后看出了普鲁士的战争挑衅。可是——据说——「法兰西不能容许这样的事，所以霍亨索伦家若一意孤行，那就是明明白白的挑战」。这个我懂不了；但别的方面我倒不忧心。我们收到柏林来信，消息来自一个极有见闻的方面：宫廷对霍亨索伦家继承西班牙王位一事，毫不在意。于是，我们操心自家房子的工程，远过于操心政治。
可是渐渐地，我们还是留意起这件事来。正如风暴来临之前，林中会起一阵叶子的萧萧声，战争来临之前，世上也会响起某种人声的窸窣。「*Nous aurons la guerre*——*nous aurons la guerre*」（我们要有战争了——我们要有战争了），这就是那时巴黎空气里的回声。于是一种说不出的焦虑攫住了我。不是为我的同胞——因为我们奥地利人，起初还算局外人。

===Original===

On the contrary, we might possibly have some “satisfaction” offered to us﻿—the well-known “revenge for Sadowa.” But we had untaught ourselves the habit of looking at war from a national point of view; and what war is from the point of view of humanity﻿—of the highest humanity﻿—is surely notorious. That is expressed in the following words which I heard spoken by Guy de Maupassant:﻿—

> “Quand je songe seulement à ce mot ‘la guerre’ il me vient un effarement, comme si l’on me parlait de sorcellerie, d’inquisition, d’une chose lontaine, finie, abominable, contre nature.”

When the news arrived that the crown had been offered by Prim to Prince Leopold, the Duke of Grammont made a speech in Parliament, which was received with great approbation, to the following effect:﻿—

> “We do not meddle with the affairs of foreign nations, but we do not believe that respect for the rights of a neighbouring state binds us to permit a foreign power, by seating one of its own princes on the throne of Charles V, to destroy, to our detriment, the equilibrium which exists between the states of Europe (Oh that equilibrium! What war-loving hypocrite invented that hollow phrase?), and so bring into danger the interests, the honour of France.”

===Chinese===

不但如此，说不定还有人要来向我们奉上一份「满足」呢——那著名的「萨多瓦复仇」。可我们早已把从民族视角看战争的习惯戒掉了；而战争从人类的视角——最高意义上的人类的视角——看是什么，想必是尽人皆知的。下面这几句话把它说了出来，是我亲耳听莫泊桑说的：——

> 「哪怕只想一想『战争』这个词，一阵惊恐便袭上我身，仿佛有人同我谈起了巫术、宗教裁判所，谈起一件遥远的、完结了的、可憎的、违反天性的东西。」

普里姆把王位授予利奥波德亲王的消息传来后，格拉蒙公爵在议会上发表了一篇演说，大获喝彩，大意如下：——

> 「我们不过问外国的内政，但我们不相信，尊重邻邦的权利竟会约束我们，容许一个外国强权把它自家的亲王安上查理五世的宝座，从而损害我们、毁掉欧洲各国之间的均势（啊，又是均势！这空洞的辞句是哪个好战的伪君子发明的？），进而置法兰西的利益与荣誉于危险之中。」

===Original===

I know a tale of George Sand named *Gribouille*. This Gribouille has the peculiarity, when rain is threatened, of plunging into the river, for fear of getting wet. Whenever I hear that war is contemplated in order to avert threatened dangers, I can never help thinking of Gribouille. A whole branch of Hohenzollerns might very well have seated themselves on Charles V’s throne, and many other thrones as well, without exposing the interests or the honour of France to one thousandth part of the damage that resulted to them from this bold “We cannot permit it.”
“The case,” the speaker continued, “will, as we most confidently believe, not occur. We reckon, in this regard, on the wisdom of the German and the friendship of the Spanish people. But if it should turn out otherwise, *then*, gentlemen, we, strong in your support and that of the nation, shall know how to do our duty, without vacillation and without weakness.” (Loud applause.)
From that time began in the press the cry for war. It was Girardin in particular, who could not inflame his countrymen sufficiently to punish the unheard-of audacity contained in this candidature for the throne. It would be unworthy of the dignity of France not to interpose her veto upon it. Prussia, it is true, would not give in, for she is bent, mad as she is, on conjuring up war. Intoxicated by her success of 1866, she believes that she may extend her march of victory and robbery on the Rhine also; but, thank God, we are ready to baulk all these appetites of the *Pickelhaubers*. And so it went on, in the same key. Napoleon III, it is true, as we found out through persons who were about him, still wished, as before, for the preservation of peace; but most of the people of his entourage now thought that a war was inevitable﻿—that, since apart from all this there was discontent among the people with the Government, the best thing that could be done to secure the respect of the country, anxious as it was for glory, would be to carry out a successful war. “*Il faut faire grand.*”
And now inquiries were made of all the European Cabinets about the situation. Each declared that they wished for peace. In Germany a manifesto was published, originating in popular articles signed by Liebknecht amongst others, wherein it was said “the mere thought of a war between Germany and France is a crime.”

===Chinese===

我知道乔治·桑写的一个故事，名叫《格里布伊》。这格里布伊有个怪脾气：一听说要下雨，就扑通跳进河里，生怕淋湿。每逢我听说有人打算用战争去防止将临的危险，就禁不住想起格里布伊。霍亨索伦全家满可以坐上查理五世的宝座，外加许多别的宝座，也不至于让法兰西的利益和荣誉受到这大胆的一句「我们不能容许」所带来损失的千分之一。
「这一情形，」演说的人继续说，「我们深信不会发生。在这一点上，我们指望德意志民族的智慧与西班牙民族的友谊。可倘若事与愿违，那么，诸位，有你们和全国人民做后盾，我们知道怎样尽我们的责任，不动摇，不软弱。」（热烈掌声。）
从那时起，报界开始了战争的叫嚣。尤其是吉拉尔丹，他鼓动同胞去惩罚这王位候选里闻所未闻的狂妄，怎么鼓动都嫌不够。法兰西若不对此行使否决，便有失尊严。普鲁士，诚然，是不会让步的，因为它疯了心，一门心思要变出一场战争来。1866年的胜利冲昏了它的头，它以为它那胜利与劫掠的进军还可以推进到莱茵河上；可是感谢上帝，我们已经准备好，要挫一挫这些尖顶盔们的全部胃口。诸如此类，同一调门，一直唱下去。拿破仑三世呢——这是我们从他身边的人们那里打听出来的——诚然仍同先前一样愿保和平；可他周围的人，如今大多认为战争不可避免——而且，撇开这一切不说，民间本就对政府有不满，那么要赢得这个渴慕荣耀的国家的敬重，最好的办法莫过于打一场成功的战争。「*Il faut faire grand*」——要干就干大的。
于是各国向欧洲各内阁探询局势。每一国都声明愿意和平。德国发表了一篇宣言，起自李卜克内西等人署名的大众文章，其中说道：「德法之间居然想到战争，这本身就是一桩罪恶。」

===Original===

Benedetti was sent with the charge of demanding from the King of Prussia that he would forbid Prince Leopold to assume the crown. King William was at that moment taking the waters at Ems. Benedetti went there, and got an audience on July 9.
What would the result be? I waited for the news with trembling.
The answer of the king simply said that he could not forbid anything to a prince who had attained adult years.
This answer sent the war party into triumphant joy. “There﻿—will you suffer that? Do they want to provoke us to the utmost? That the head of the house cannot command or forbid anything to one of its members! Ridiculous! It is clearly a made-up plot﻿—the Hohenzollerns want to get a footing in Spain, and then fall upon our country from the east and south at once. And are we to wait for that? Are we to be content to take with humility the utter disregard of our protest? Surely not. We know what honour, what patriotism, commands us to do.”
Ever louder and louder, ever more and more threatening sounded the storm-warnings. Then on July 12 came a piece of news which filled me with delight. Don Salusto Olozaga announced officially to the French Government that Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern, in order not to give any pretext for war, refused to assume the crown offered to him.
Now, thank God, the entire “question” is thus simply put aside. The news was communicated to the Chamber at 12 at noon, and Ollivier declared that this put an end to the dispute. Yet, on the same day, troops and war material were forwarded to Metz (publicly said to be in pursuance of previous orders), and in the same sitting Clement Duvernois put the following question:﻿—

> “What securities have we that Prussia will not originate fresh complications, like this Spanish candidature? That should be provided against.”

===Chinese===

贝内德蒂奉命出发，去向普鲁士国王要求：禁止利奥波德亲王接受王位。威廉国王那时正在埃姆斯疗养。贝内德蒂去了那里，7月9日得了觐见。
结果会怎样呢？我战栗着等候消息。
国王的回答很简单：对一位已成年的亲王，他无从禁止什么。
这个回答使主战派陷入了胜利的狂欢。「瞧吧——这你们也能忍？他们是要把我们挑衅到极处么？一家之长竟不能命令或禁止自家成员任何事情！可笑！这明明是设好的圈套——霍亨索伦家想在西班牙落脚，然后从东、南两面立刻扑向我们国家。难道我们要坐等吗？难道我们该谦卑地咽下他们对我们抗议的全然无视？断乎不可。荣誉要求我们做什么，爱国心要求我们做什么，我们知道。」
风暴的警报一声高过一声，一次比一次吓人。随后，7月12日来了一条消息，使我满心欢喜。堂萨卢斯托·奥洛萨加向法国政府正式宣布：霍亨索伦的利奥波德亲王为了不给战争留任何借口，拒绝接受已向他提出的王位。
好了，感谢上帝，整个「问题」就这样轻轻撇开了。消息于正午12时报知议院，奥利维耶宣告争端就此了结。然而就在同一天，军队和作战物资被运往梅斯（公开的说法是执行先前的命令）；同一次会议上，克莱芒·迪韦尔努瓦提出了下面这个问题：——

> 「我们有什么担保，普鲁士不会再制造像这次西班牙候选一样的新纠纷？这必须预先防到。」

===Original===

There Gribouille comes up again. It may happen, perhaps, at some time, that a trifling rain may threaten to wet us; so let us jump into the river at once!
And so Benedetti was despatched again to Ems; this time to demand of the King of Prussia that he would forbid Prince Leopold once for all, and for all future time, to revive his candidature. What could follow such an attempt at dictating a course of action, which the party on whom the demand is made is not competent to carry out, except an impatient shrug of the shoulders? Those who made the demand must have known as much.
There was another memorable sitting on July 15. Ollivier demanded a credit of 500,000,000 frs. for the war. *Thiers opposed it.* Ollivier replied. He took on himself to justify before the bar of history what had been done. The King of Prussia had refused to receive the French envoy, and had notified this to the Government in a letter. The Left wanted to see this letter. The majority forbade, by clamour and by a counter-vote, the production of the document, which probably had no existence. This majority supported any demand made by the Government in favour of the war. This patriotic readiness for sacrifice, which would accept even *ruin* without hesitation, was of course again applauded becomingly with the usual ready-made turns of sentence.
July 16. England made attempts to prevent the war. In vain. Ah! if there had been an arbitration court established how easily and simply might such a trivial dispute have been decided.
July 19. The French chargé d’affaires in Berlin handed the Prussian Government the declaration of war.
Declaration of war! Three words, which can be pronounced quite calmly. But what is connected with them? The beginning of an extra-political action, and thus, along with it, half-a-million sentences of death.
This document also I entered in the red volumes. It runs thus:﻿—

===Chinese===

格里布伊又来了。说不定什么时候，一场毛毛雨也许威胁着要打湿我们；那我们赶紧跳河吧！
于是贝内德蒂再度被派往埃姆斯；这一回是要求普鲁士国王一劳永逸地禁止利奥波德亲王日后重新提出候选。这样一种发号施令——要求对方去做一件他无权做到的事——除了换来一声不耐烦的耸肩，还能有什么结果？提出要求的人对此不可能不明白。
7月15日又是一次难忘的会议。奥利维耶为战争要求5亿法郎的拨款。*梯也尔反对。*奥利维耶答辩。他把已经做出的事，担到历史法庭面前去辩护。他说普鲁士国王拒绝接见法国使节，并已致函通知政府。左派要求看这封信。多数派用鼓噪和表决压下了这份文件的出示——那文件多半根本不存在。这个多数派支持政府提出的每一项利于战争的要求。这种连*毁灭*也毫不犹豫地照单全收的爱国牺牲精神，自然又博得了得体的掌声，外加一套现成的套话。
7月16日。英国试图阻止战争。徒劳。啊！倘若早已设立了仲裁法庭，这样一桩鸡毛蒜皮的争端，本可以何等轻易、何等简单地裁决。
7月19日。法国驻柏林代办向普鲁士政府递交了宣战书。
宣战！三个字，可以平平静静地说出口。可与它连在一起的是什么？一项超乎政治的行动的开端，随之而来的，是五十万份死刑判决。
这份文书我也录进了红皮日记本。原文如下：——

===Original===

> The Government of His Majesty the Emperor of the French could not regard the design of raising a Prussian prince to the throne of Spain otherwise than as an attack on the territorial security of France, and has therefore found itself compelled to request from His Majesty the King of Prussia the assurance that such a combination should never again occur with his consent. As His Majesty refuses any such assurance, and has, on the contrary, declared to our ambassador that he must reserve to himself the possibility of such an event, and inquire into the circumstances, the Imperial Government cannot help recognising in this declaration of the king an arrière-pensée, which, for France and for the European equilibrium﻿ ﻿… (There it comes again﻿—this famous equilibrium. Look at this shelf, and the precious china on it﻿—it is tottering; the dishes may fall, so let us smash it down.) This declaration has assumed a still graver character from the communication which has been made to the Cabinet of the refusal to receive the emperor’s ambassador, and to introduce, in common with him, a new method of solution. (So, by such things as these, by a more or less friendly conversation between rulers and diplomatists, the fate of nations may be decided.) In consequence of this the French Government has thought it its duty (!) without delay to think of the defence (Yes, yes, defence: never attack) of its outraged dignity and its outraged interests, and being determined to employ for that end all means which are offered by the position which has been imposed upon it, regards itself from this time forward as in a state of war with Prussia.

===Chinese===

> 法兰西皇帝陛下的政府，只能把将一位普鲁士亲王推上西班牙王位的图谋视为对法兰西领土安全的攻击，因此不得不请普鲁士国王陛下作出保证：此类情事永不因其允诺而再度发生。由于陛下拒绝任何此类保证，且反而向我国大使表示，他必须为此类事件的可能性自留余地、查明情由，帝国政府在此国王宣言中便不能不认出一层隐衷，它于法兰西、于欧洲均势……（又来了——这著名的均势。瞧瞧这只搁架，和架上的名贵瓷器——它晃了；盘子也许会掉下来，那咱们干脆把它整个砸了算了。）由于内阁接到通知：对方拒绝接见皇帝的大使、拒绝与大使共同引入新的解决办法，这一宣言的性质就愈发严重了。（瞧，凭这样的东西，凭君主与外交家之间一场或亲或疏的谈话，各民族的命运就这样被决定。）有鉴于此，法国政府认为它有责任（！）毫不迟疑地考虑其受辱的尊严与受辱的利益的防卫（是的，是的，防卫：从来不是进攻），并决意为此动用强加于它的处境所提供的一切手段，自即日起视自己为同普鲁士处于战争状态。

===Original===

State of war! Does the man think who puts these words on paper, on the green cloth of his writing-table, that he is plunging his pen in flames, in tears of blood, in the poison of plague?
And so the storm is unchained, this time on account of a king being sought for a vacant throne, and as the consequence of a negotiation undertaken between two monarchs! Must Kant then be right in his first definitive condition for everlasting peace? “The civil constitution in every state should be republican.” To be sure, the effect of this article would be to remove many causes of war; for history shows how many campaigns have been undertaken for dynastic questions, and the whole establishment of monarchical power rests assuredly on successful conduct of war﻿—still republics also are warlike. It is the *spirit*, the old savage spirit which lights up hatred, lust of plunder, and ambition of conquest in peoples, whether governed in one form or another.
I recollect what an altogether peculiar humour seized me at this time, when the Franco-German war was in preparation and then broke out. The stormy sultriness before, the howling tempest after its declaration. The whole population was in a fever, and who can keep himself aloof from such an epidemic? Naturally, according to old custom, the beginning of the campaign was at once looked on as a triumphal procession﻿—that is no more than patriotic duty. “*À Berlin, à Berlin*,” was shouted through the streets and from the outside of the omnibusses﻿—the Marseillaise at every street corner, “*Le jour de gloire est arrivé.*” At every theatrical representation the first actress or singer, at the opera it was Marie Sass, had to come before the curtain in a Jeanne d’Arc costume, waving a flag, and sing this battle song, which was received by the audience standing, and in which they often joined. We also were among the spectators one evening, Frederick and I, and we also had to rise from our seats. I say “had to,” not from any external pressure, for we could of course have withdrawn into the back of the box, but “had to,” because we were *electrified*.
“Look, Martha,” Frederick explained to me, “a spark like that which runs from one man to another and makes this whole mass rise to one united and excited heartbeat, that is *love*.”
“What do you mean? It is surely a song of hatred:﻿—

> That their unholy blood

May sink into our furrows.”

===Chinese===

战争状态！把这几个字落到纸上的人——落在书桌的绿呢面上——可曾想过，他是在把笔插进火焰里，插进血泪里，插进瘟疫的毒液里？
于是风暴解开了锁链，这一回，是因为一顶空王冠要找主人，因为两位君主之间的一场交涉！难道康德竟然是对的吗——他关于永久和平的第一项正式条款：「每个国家的公民宪法都应当是共和制的。」诚然，这一条会消除许多战争的起因；历史表明，多少次战役是为王朝问题打的，而君主权力这整套建制，确乎奠立于战争的顺利进行——可是共和国也照样好战。关键在*精神*，是那古老的野蛮精神，在各族人民心里点燃仇恨、掠夺欲与征服欲，无论政体是这一种还是那一种。
我记得，德法战争酝酿继而爆发的那段日子，一种全然特别的心绪攫住了我。先前是风暴前的闷热，宣战之后是呼啸的狂飙。全城的人都在发烧，这样一场时疫，谁躲得开？自然，照老规矩，开仗立刻被看成了凯旋游行——这不过是爱国义务。「*À Berlin，à Berlin*」（到柏林去，到柏林去），满街、连公共马车的车厢外都这样喊——每个街角都是马赛曲，「*Le jour de gloire est arrivé*」（光荣的日子到了）。每一场演出，头牌女演员或歌手——歌剧院里是玛丽·萨丝——都得穿上圣女贞德的装束，挥着一面旗，到幕前唱这支战歌；听众肃立受之，还常常跟着唱。一天晚上，腓特烈和我也在观众席上，我们也只得从座位上站起来。我说「只得」，不是出于任何外来的压力——我们自然可以退到包厢后头去——而是「只得」，因为我们被*电着了*。
「你瞧，玛尔塔，」腓特烈向我解释道，「这样的火花，从一个人身上窜到另一个人身上，使这一整个人群同一个共同的、激越的心跳一齐立起——这就是爱。」
「你这话怎么讲？这分明是一支仇恨的歌：——

> 愿他们不洁的血液
> 浸进我们的犁沟。」

===Original===

“That is no matter, united hatred also is one form of love. Wherever two or more unite in one common feeling, they love each other. Let but a higher conception than that of the nation, i.e., of mankind and of humanity, once be seized as the general idea, and then﻿—”
“Ah,” I sighed, “when will that be?”
“When? that is a very relative term. In regard to the duration of our life, never; in regard to that of our race, tomorrow.”
---
When war has broken out all the subjects of neutral states divide themselves into two camps, one takes the side of the one, the other of the opposite party; it is like a great fluctuating wager, in which everyone has a share.
We too﻿—Frederick and I﻿—with which side should we sympathise, which wish to conquer? As Austrians we should have been fully justified, “patriotically,” in wishing to see our victor in the former war vanquished in this one. Besides, it is again natural that one should give the greater sympathy to those in whose midst one is living, and with whose feelings one is involuntarily infected; and we were then surrounded by the French. Still, Frederick was of Prussian descent, and were we not more allied with the Germans, whose speech even was my own, than with their adversaries? Besides, had not the declaration of war proceeded from the French, on such trifling grounds﻿—nay, not grounds, but pretexts? And must we not conclude from that that the Prussian cause was the more just one, and that they were going into battle only as defenders, and in obedience to compulsion? King William had spoken with much justice in his speech from the throne on July 19:﻿—

> The German and the French nations, both enjoying equally the blessings of Christian training and increasing prosperity, have been called to a more holy strife than the bloody one of arms. The rulers of France, however, have contrived to make profit for their own personal interests and passions out of the justifiable but irritable self-consciousness of our great neighbour by means of deliberate deception.

The Emperor Napoleon, on his side, published the following proclamation:﻿—

===Chinese===

「那不要紧，联合起来的仇恨也是爱的一种形态。凡两人或多人结合于一个共同的情感，他们便是彼此相爱。只消让一个比民族更高的概念——也就是人类与人道的概念——被抓住，成为普遍的理念，那时——」
「唉，」我叹道，「那要到什么时候呢？」
「什么时候？这是个很相对的说法。以我们一生的长度论，永远不会；以我们种族的长度论，就在明天。」
---
战争一经爆发，一切中立国的臣民便分作两营，一营向着这一方，一营向着那一方；像一场浮动的大赌局，人人都有一份。
我们呢——腓特烈和我——该同情哪一边，盼哪一边赢呢？作为奥地利人，「爱国地」盼着上一回战胜我们的那一方这一回被打败，我们原是全然有理的。再说，人自然也更同情生活在其中的人们，不由自主地被他们的情绪感染；而我们那时正被法国人包围着。可是腓特烈毕竟是普鲁士血统；何况，同他们的对手相比，我们不是同德意志人更亲近么——连语言也是我的母语？再说，宣战难道不是法国人先提出的么，理由那样微不足道——不，那不是理由，是借口？由此我们岂不应当断定，普鲁士的事业更正当些，他们是只作为防御者、迫于无奈才上阵的？威廉国王7月19日的御座演说，说得很有公道：——

> 德意志与法兰西两大民族，同享基督教教化的福泽，同沐日益增长的繁荣，本被召唤去进行一场比兵戎相见的血战更神圣的角逐。然而法兰西的统治者们，处心积虑地施骗，利用我们伟大邻邦那正当而急躁的自尊，为一己的利益与情欲谋利。

拿破仑皇帝那边，则发布了如下的公告：——

===Original===

> In view of the presumptuous pretensions of Prussia, we were obliged to make protests. These were treated with scorn. Transactions9 followed which showed their contempt for us. Our country has been deeply irritated at this, and at present the cry for war resounds from one end of France to the other. There remains nothing possible for us except to trust our fate to the arbitrament of arms. We are not making war on Germany, whose independence we respect. It is the object of our best wishes that the people composing the great German nationality should dispose freely of their own fate. As far as concerns ourselves, we desire to set up a state of things which will guarantee our security and make our future safe. We wish to obtain a lasting peace, founded on the true interests of the peoples. We wish for the termination of this miserable situation, in which all the nations are expending their resources in arming on all sides against each other.

===Chinese===

> 面对普鲁士狂妄的要求，我们不得不提出抗议。抗议被轻蔑地对待。继之而来的种种行径，更表明了他们对我们的蔑视。我国为此深深激愤，如今战争的呐喊正从法兰西的一端响到另一端。我们别无他途，只能把命运托付给武器的裁决。我们不是对德意志作战——德意志的独立，我们是尊重的。组成伟大德意志民族的各族人民能自由支配自己的命运，正是我们最良好的愿望所在。至于我们自己，我们希望建立一种局面，保障我们的安全，确保我们的未来。我们希望获得持久的和平——奠基于各民族真正利益之上的和平。我们希望终止这可悲的局面：一切民族彼此四面设防，把资财挥霍殆尽。

===Original===

What a lesson! what a mighty lesson speaks from this writing, when compared with the events which ensued upon it! This campaign, then, was undertaken by France in order to attain security﻿—to attain lasting peace? And what came of it? *L’annèe terrible* and lasting enmity﻿—enmity which still prevails. No; as with coal you cannot whitewash, as with asafoetida you cannot diffuse a sweet perfume, so neither with war can you make peace secure. This “miserable situation,” to which Napoleon alludes, how much has it not changed for the worse since then! The emperor was in earnest, thoroughly in earnest about the scheme for setting on foot a European disarmament. I have it quite certainly from his nearest relations; but the war party put pressure on him﻿—coerced him﻿—and he yielded. And yet he could not refrain, even in the war proclamation, from harping on his favourite idea. Its carrying out was only to be deferred. “After the campaign”﻿—“after the victory,” said he, to console himself. It turned out otherwise.
So, on which side were our sympathies? If one has got to the point of detesting all war in and for itself, as was the case with Frederick and me, the genuine, pure, “passionate attachment” to either side can exist no more. One’s only feeling is “Oh that it had never begun﻿—this campaign! Oh that it were only already over!”
I did not think that the existing war would last long, or have important consequences. Two or three battles won here and there, and then there would be parleys for certain, and the thing would be brought to an end. What were they really fighting for? Literally for nothing. The whole thing was more of an armed promenade, undertaken by the French from love of knightly adventure, by the Germans from brave feelings of defensive duty. A few sabre-cuts would be exchanged, and the adversaries would shake hands again. Fool that I was! As if the consequences of a war remained in any proportion to the causes which produced it. It is its *course* which determines its consequences.
We should have been glad to leave Paris, for all the enthusiasm which the whole population displayed produced the most painful effect on us. But the way eastward was barred for the present, and the business of our house-building detained us. In short, we stayed. We had hardly any society connections left.

===Chinese===

何等的一课！这篇文告同随后发生的事件一对照，其中说出了何等有力的一课！这么说，法兰西发动这场战役，是为了求得安全——求得持久的和平？结果得到了什么？《可怕的一年》（*L'année terrible*）和持久的仇恨——至今犹存的仇恨。不；正如用煤刷不了白墙，用阿魏熏不出甜香，用战争也保不了和平。拿破仑提到的那「可悲的局面」，从那以后又恶化了多少啊！皇帝是认真的，对发起全欧裁军的计划彻头彻尾地认真；这一点我从他至亲那里知道得千真万确；可是主战派压他——胁迫他——他让步了。即便在宣战公告里，他仍忍不住重弹他心爱的调子：那计划的实行不过推迟而已。「等这一仗打完」——「等胜利以后」，他这样宽解自己。结果却是另一回事。
那么，我们的同情在哪一边呢？当一个人已经到了憎恶一切战争本身的境地——腓特烈和我便是如此——那么对这一边或那一边的真正的、纯粹的「热烈拥戴」，便再也不存在了。剩下的感觉只是：「唉，但愿这仗压根没打起来！唉，但愿它已经打完了才好！」
我原以为眼下的战争打不长，也不会有重大后果。这边那边赢上两三仗，然后必定谈判，事情就了结了。他们究竟为什么打？说实在的，什么都不为。整件事更像一次武装的散步：法国人出于对骑士奇遇的爱好，德国人出于勇敢的防御责任感。交锋几个回合，交战双方重新握手。我这个傻瓜！仿佛战争的后果会同它的起因成什么比例似的。决定其后果的，是它的*进程*。
我们本乐意离开巴黎，因为全城表露的那股狂热，在我们心里产生最痛苦的效果。可东去的路一时不通，造房的工程又绊着我们。总之，我们留下了。社交的关系几乎断尽了。

===Original===

Everybody that could anyhow do so had fled from Paris; and even of those who remained, no one under present circumstances even thought of issuing invitations. A few, however, of our acquaintances among the literary circles, who were still in the city, we did frequently visit. Just at this phase of the commencing war, it interested Frederick to make himself acquainted with the judgments and views then entertained by the master spirits of the time. There was an author, then quite young, who later on attained much fame, Guy de Maupassant, some of whose utterances, which penetrated into my soul, I entered in the red volumes:﻿—

> War﻿—if I only think of the word a horror comes over me, as if people were talking to me about witches, about the inquisition, about some faraway, overmastering, horrible, unnatural thing. War﻿—to fight each other, strangle, cut each other to pieces! And we have amongst us at this day, in our times, with our culture, with such an extension of science, with so high a grade of development as we believe ourselves to have attained﻿—we have schools, where people are taught to kill, to kill at a good distance, and a good round number at a time. What is wonderful is that the people do not rise up against it, that the whole of society does not revolt at the bare word﻿—war!
> Every man who governs is just as much bound to avoid war as a ship’s captain is bound to avoid shipwreck. If a captain has lost a ship he is brought before a court and tried, so that it may be known whether he has been guilty of negligence. Why should not a Government be put on its trial whenever a war has been declared? If the people understood it, if they refused to allow themselves to be killed without cause, there would be an end of war.

I had also an opportunity of reading a letter, written by Gustave Flaubert to George Sand in the early days of July, just after the outbreak of the war. Here it is:﻿—

===Chinese===

凡是能够走的，都逃出了巴黎；留下的这些人里，眼下也没有谁想着请客了。不过文艺圈的几位相识还在城里，我们倒常去看望。正逢战争初起的这个阶段，腓特烈很有兴味去了解当时第一流头脑们所持的判断和见解。有一位作家，那时还十分年轻，后来名声大噪——居伊·德·莫泊桑——他的几段话渗进了我的灵魂，我录进了红皮日记本：——

> 战争——我只要想一想这个词，恐怖便压上心来，仿佛人们在同我谈论巫婆、宗教裁判所，谈论某种遥远的、久已过去的、可怕而不自然的东西。战争——互相厮杀、扼喉、碎尸！而我们今天，在我们这个时代，以我们的文化，以如此扩张的科学，以我们自信已达到的如此高度的发展——我们居然办着学校，教人杀人，教人在老远的距离杀人，一次杀它结结实实的一大串。奇怪的是人民不起来反抗它，整个社会竟不因「战争」这个赤裸裸的词而哗然！
> 凡执掌治理之权的人，同船长之必须避免船难一样，有同等的义务避免战争。船长损失了一条船，就要到法庭受审，查明他是否有过失。为什么每逢一场战争被宣布，政府不该同样受审？倘若人民懂得了这一点，倘若他们拒绝平白无故地让人杀死，战争就到头了。

我还得到机会读到一封信，是居斯塔夫·福楼拜在7月初、战争刚爆发时写给乔治·桑的。信如下：——

===Original===

> I am in despair at the stupidity of my countrymen. The incorrigible barbarity of men fills me with deep grief. This enthusiasm, which is inspired by no idea, makes me wish to die in order to see no more of it. These good Frenchmen wish to fight (1) because they believe themselves challenged by Prussia, (2) because savagery is the natural state of men, (3) because war has an element of mystery in it which is alluring to men. Are we coming to indiscriminate fighting? I fear it.﻿ ﻿… The horrible battles which are in preparation have no pretext whatever for them. It is the love of fighting for fighting’s sake. I lament for the bridges and tunnels blown up. All this human labour gone to ruin. You will have seen that a gentleman recommended in the Chamber the plundering of the Grand Duchy of Baden. Oh that I could be with the Bedouins!

“Oh,” cried I, as I read this letter, “that we could have been born 500 years later! that would be even better than the Bedouins.”
“Men will not want all that time to become reasonable,” said Frederick confidently.
---
The period of proclamations and general orders was now come.
The old humdrum tune again always, and always again the public carried away to give it support and enthusiasm! There was joy over the victories guaranteed in the manifestoes, just as if they had been gained already.
On July 28 Napoleon III issued the following document from his headquarters at Metz. This also I entered in my book, not, indeed, because I shared in the admiration but from contempt for the everlasting sameness and hollowness of its phrase-mongering:﻿—

> We are defending the honour and the soil of our country. We shall conquer. Nothing is too much for the persevering exertions of the soldiers of Africa, the Crimea, China, Italy and Mexico: Once more you will show what a French army can do, which is on fire with the love of country. Whatever way we take out of our boundaries, we find there the glorious footsteps of our forefathers. We will show ourselves worthy of them. On our success depends the fate of Freedom and Civilisation. Soldiers! let everyone do his duty, and the God of Battles will be with us.

===Chinese===

> 我对我的同胞们的愚蠢感到绝望。人类无可救药的野蛮使我充满深哀。这股不为任何思想所激发的狂热，叫我但愿一死，免得再看下去。这些善良的法国人想打仗：（一）因为他们相信自己受了普鲁士的挑衅；（二）因为野蛮是人的天然状态；（三）因为战争里有一种神秘的成分，对人颇有诱惑。我们是不是正走向不分青红皂白的厮杀？我怕是。……正在酝酿的那些可怕战役，没有任何借口可言。这是为打而打的爱。我为被炸毁的桥梁和隧道悲叹。这一切人的劳作，尽成废墟。想来您已见到，有位先生在议院里建议劫掠巴登大公国。啊，我宁可同贝都因人在一起！

「哦，」我读着信喊道，「但愿我们晚生500年！那可比同贝都因人在一起还要好。」
「用不了那么久，人就会变得理性。」腓特烈满有把握地说。
---
接下来是公告与军令的时期。
永远是那套陈腔老调，而公众永远又被它卷走，去给它支持和热情！宣言里担保的胜利已经引起了欢腾，仿佛胜利已经到手。
7月28日，拿破仑三世在梅斯大本营发布了下面的文告。这份我也录进了本子——不是因为共鸣，而是出于对那套永远雷同、空空如也的滥调的鄙夷：——

> 我们在保卫国家的荣誉与国土。我们必将胜利。非洲、克里米亚、中国、意大利和墨西哥的老兵们坚韧不拔，什么都当得起：你们将再一次显示，一支燃烧着爱国之火的法国军队有何能为。我们无论从哪里跨出国界，脚下都是先辈光荣的足迹。我们要证明自己无愧于他们。自由与文明的命运，系于我们的胜利。士兵们！人人恪尽职守，战神上帝必与我们同在。

===Original===

Of course, “*le Dieu des Armées*” could not be left out. That the leaders of defeated armies have said the same thing a hundred times over does not prevent the others from saying the same words at the beginning of every new campaign and awakening the same confidence by doing so. Is there anything more short and more weak than the memory of the people?
On July 31 King William quitted Berlin and left the following writing:﻿—

> In going today to the army, to fight along with it for honour and for the preservation of our noblest possessions, I leave an amnesty for all political offenders. My people know as well as I that the breach of treaty and hostile proceedings are not on our side. But as we have been provoked, we are determined, like our fathers, and in firm reliance on God, to brave the battle for the deliverance of our fatherland.

===Chinese===

当然，「万军之上帝」（*le Dieu des Armées*）是不能漏掉的。败军的统帅们把同样的话说过一百遍，这也拦不住另外一些人在每场新战役开始时说同样的话，并借此唤起同样的信心。还有比人民的记忆更短、更靠不住的东西吗？
7月31日，威廉国王离开柏林，留下了下面这纸文字：——

> 今日朕赴军中，与之并肩为荣誉、为我们最珍贵的产业之保全而战；朕于此赦免一切政治犯。朕之人民同朕一样知道：违约与挑衅之举，不在我方。然我等既遭挑衅，便决意一如我父辈，坚定依赖上帝，为祖国之解救奋身赴战。

===Original===

Necessity of defence﻿—necessity of defence﻿—that is the only recognised way of killing, and so both parties cry out: “I am defending myself.” Is not that a contradiction? Not altogether, for over both there presides a third power, the power of the conquering, ancient war-spirit. It is only against *him* that all should join in a defensive league.
Along with the above manifestoes, I find in my red volumes an entry, with the singular title written over it: “If Ollivier had married Meyerbeer’s daughter would the war have broken out?” This is how the matter stood. Amongst our Parisian acquaintance there was a literary man named Alexander Weill, and it was he who threw out the above question, while he told us the following story:﻿—
“Meyerbeer was looking out for a man of talent for his second daughter, and his choice fell on my friend Emile Ollivier. Ollivier was a widower. He had married for his first wife the daughter of Liszt, whom the renowned pianist had by the Countess d’Agoult (Daniel Stern), with whom he long lived as his wife. The marriage was very happy, and Ollivier had the reputation of a virtuous husband. He possessed no fortune, but as a speaker and statesman he was already famous. Meyerbeer wanted to make his personal acquaintance, and to this end I gave, in April, 1864, a great ball, which was attended by most of the celebrities of art and science, and where, of course, Ollivier, who had been informed by me of Meyerbeer’s purpose, played the first part. He pleased Meyerbeer. The matter was not easy to bring to a head. Meyerbeer knew the independent originality of his second daughter, who would never marry any other husband than one of her own choice. It was arranged that Ollivier should pay a visit to Baden, and there be introduced as if by chance to the young lady. When Meyerbeer died suddenly a fortnight after this ball, it was Ollivier, if you recollect, who pronounced his *éloge* and funeral oration at the Northern Railway Station. Now, I affirm, nay I am certain of it, that if Ollivier had married Meyerbeer’s daughter, the war between France and Germany would not have broken out. Look how plausible my proofs are. In the first place, Meyerbeer, who hated the empire to the point of contempt, would never have permitted his daughter’s husband to become a minister of the emperor.

===Chinese===

防御之必要——防御之必要——这是唯一得到公认的杀人之道，于是交战双方齐声大喊：「我是在自卫。」这不是矛盾么？不全然是，因为两造之上还坐着一个第三势力——那战无不胜的古老战争精神的势力。唯独对*它*，才应当人人结成防御同盟。
在上录各宣言之外，我在红皮日记本里还找到一条记载，头上题着一个古怪的题目：「倘若奥利维耶娶了迈耶贝尔的女儿，战争还会打起来吗？」事情是这样。我们巴黎的相识里有一位文人，名唤亚历山大·魏尔，上面这个问题就是他抛出来的，他一面给我们讲了下面这段故事：——
「迈耶贝尔正为他的二女儿物色一个有才华的女婿，他看中了我的朋友埃米尔·奥利维耶。奥利维耶是鳏夫。他的元配是李斯特的女儿——那位名钢琴家与达古尔伯爵夫人（丹尼尔·斯特恩）所生，李斯特同她以夫妻之实同居多年。那桩婚姻很美满，奥利维耶享有贤夫的美名。他没有财产，但作为演说家和政治家已负盛名。迈耶贝尔想同他亲自结识，为此我在1864年4月办了一场盛大的舞会，文艺科学界的名流到了大半；奥利维耶呢——我已把迈耶贝尔的意思告知了他——自然在会上做了头号角色。他中迈耶贝尔的意了。这事却不容易推到头。迈耶贝尔深知二女儿那份独立的个性，她非自己看中的人，谁也不嫁。于是安排奥利维耶到巴登去小住，在那里被『偶然』引见给这位小姐。舞会后两星期，迈耶贝尔猝然去世；您总记得，在北火车站致悼词、唱颂歌的，正是奥利维耶。如今我断言——不，我确信——倘若奥利维耶娶了迈耶贝尔的女儿，法德之间的战争就不会打起来。瞧我的论证多么站得住。第一，迈耶贝尔对帝国的憎恶近乎轻蔑，他绝不会容许自己的女婿去当皇帝的大臣。

===Original===

It is well known that, if Ollivier had threatened the Chamber to give in his resignation sooner than declare war, the Chamber would never have declared war. The present war is the work of three backstairs confidants and secret ministers of the empress, named, Jerôme David, Paul de Cassagnac, and the Duc de Grammont. The empress, excited by the Pope, whose religious puppet she is, would have this war, as to the success of which she never doubted, in order to ensure her son’s succession. She said: ‘*C’est ma guerre à moi et à mon fils,*’ and the three above-named papal ‘anabaptists’ were her secret tools to force the emperor, who did not want any war, and the Chamber into war by false and secret despatches from Germany.”
“And this is what is called diplomacy!” I interrupted with a shudder.
“Listen further,” pursued Alexander Weill. “Ollivier said to me on July 15, when I met him on the Place de la Concorde: ‘Peace is assured, or I resign.’ Whence came it then that this same man, a few days later, instead of resigning, declared war himself, ‘*d’un cœur léger*,’ as he said in the Chamber?”
“With a light heart!” I cried, shuddering again.
“There is a secret in this that I can throw light upon. The emperor, for whom money had never any other value than to purchase love or friendship with it (he believes, like Jugurtha in Rome, that all in France, men and women, have their price), has the custom, when he takes a minister who is not rich, of binding him more closely to himself by a present of a million francs. Daru alone, who told me this secret, declined this present﻿—‘*Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes.*’ And he alone, being unfettered, sent in his resignation. As long as the emperor hesitated, Ollivier, being bound to his master by this chain of gold, declared himself neutral﻿—rather inclined to peace. But as soon as the emperor had been overborne by his wife and her three ultramontane anabaptists, Ollivier declared for war, and gave it lively utterance, with light heart, ‘and with full pockets.’ ”10

===Chinese===

「尽人皆知，倘若当时奥利维耶以辞职相胁，宁肯挂冠也不宣战，议院是绝不会宣战的。眼下的战争，出自皇后的三个幕后亲信兼秘密大臣之手：热罗姆·达维德、保罗·德·卡萨尼亚克，还有格拉蒙公爵。皇后——她本人是教皇的宗教傀儡——受了教皇的怂恿，定要打这一仗；她对胜利从不怀疑，为的是确保她儿子的继承权。她说：『*C'est ma guerre à moi et à mon fils*』（这是我和我儿子的战争）；上面那三位教皇的『再洗礼派』，便是她的秘密工具，靠来自德国的伪造密电，把不想打仗的皇帝和议院一并拖进战争。」
「这就是所谓外交！」我战栗着打断他。
「再往下听，」亚历山大·魏尔接着说，「7月15日，我在协和广场遇见奥利维耶，他对我说：『和平是笃定的，不然我就辞职。』可几天之后，同是这个人，非但不辞职，反而亲自宣了战，照他自己在议院里说的，是『*d'un cœur léger*』。」
「怀着轻快的心！」我喊道，又是一阵战栗。
「这里面有一桩秘密，我能把它照亮。皇帝其人，钱在他手里从来只有一种用处：买取爱或友谊（他像罗马时的朱古达一样相信，法兰西的一切人，无论男女，各有各的价钱）；因此他有个习惯：凡是起用不富有的大臣，便馈赠一百万法郎，把此人更牢地拴在自己身上。唯有达吕——这秘密就是他告诉我的——谢绝了这份馈赠——『*Timeo Danaos et dona ferentes*』（我惧怕希腊人，哪怕他们来献礼）。也唯有他，无牵无挂，递了辞呈。皇帝犹豫的那些日子，奥利维耶被这条金链拴在主子身上，自称中立——还偏向和平。可皇帝一旦被他的妻子和她的三个越山派再洗礼徒压服，奥利维耶便主战了，而且说得眉飞色舞，怀着轻快的心——『还有满满一口袋』。」10

## XVIII / XVIII
===Original===

First Days of the War in Paris﻿—Constant Reverses of the French Arms﻿—Fall of Metz﻿—Paris Turned Into a Fortress﻿—The Prussians Expelled from Paris﻿—Surrender of the Emperor Napoleon and His Army at Sedan﻿—Proclamation of the Republic﻿—Futile Negotiations for Peace﻿—We Determine to Quit Paris﻿—This Is Prevented by My Illness﻿—When I Recover the Winter Has Set In, and Paris Has Long Been Beleaguered﻿—Fall of Strasbourg﻿—Paris Bombarded﻿—The Proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles﻿—Dreams of Release and Future Happiness Suddenly Interrupted by the Arrest and Execution of My Husband by the Communards.
“Oh monsieur! Oh madame! What happiness! What great news!” With these words Frederick’s valet rushed into our room one day, and the cook after him. It was the day of Wörth.
“What is it?”
“A telegram has been posted up at the Bourse. We have conquered. The King of Prussia’s army is as good as annihilated. The city is adorning itself with tricolour flags. There will be an illumination tonight.”
But in the course of the afternoon it turned out that the news was false﻿—a Bourse trick. Ollivier made a speech to the crowd from his balcony. Well, so much the better; at least one would not be obliged to illuminate. These joyful tidings of “armies annihilated”﻿—i.e., of numberless lives torn asunder, and hearts broken﻿—awoke again in me too the same wish as Flaubert’s﻿—“Oh that I were with the Bedouins!”
On August 7, news of a catastrophe. The emperor hastened from St. Cloud to the theatre of war. The enemy had penetrated into the country. The newspapers could not give expression hot enough to their rage at the “invasion.” The cry “*À Berlin*,” as it seemed to me, pointed to an intended invasion; but in that there was nothing to cause anger. But that these eastern barbarians should venture to make an incursion into beautiful, God-beloved France﻿—that was sheer savagery and sin. That must be stopped, and quickly too.
The Minister of War *ad interim* published a decree that all citizens fit for service, from the age of thirty to forty, who did not belong to the National Guard, should be immediately enrolled in that body. A Ministry of the Defence of the Country was formed. The war loan of 500 millions, which had been voted, was raised to 1000. It is quite refreshing to see how freely people always offer up the money and the lives of others.

===Chinese===

战争初期在巴黎的日子——法军接连受挫——梅斯陷落——巴黎变成堡垒——普鲁士人被逐出巴黎——拿破仑皇帝及其大军在色当投降——共和国宣告成立——徒劳的和平谈判——我们决意离开巴黎——却因我病倒而受阻——待我痊愈，寒冬已至，巴黎久已被围——斯特拉斯堡陷落——巴黎遭炮击——德意志帝国在凡尔赛宣告成立——获释与未来幸福的梦，骤然被我的丈夫之被捕与被处决打断——动手的是公社社员。

「哦先生！哦夫人！多幸福啊！多大的好消息啊！」一天，弗雷德里克的贴身男仆这样嚷着冲进我们的房间，厨娘紧随其后。那是沃尔特之役的日子。

「什么事？」

「交易所门前贴出了一份电报。我们打赢了。普鲁士国王的军队等于全军覆没。全城都在张挂三色旗。今夜要燃灯庆祝。」

可是到了午后，消息证明是假的——一场交易所的把戏。奥利维耶在自家阳台上向人群发表了一通演说。也好，这样更好；至少不必被迫张灯了。这些「敌军全歼」的喜讯——也就是无数生命被撕碎、无数颗心破碎的消息——又在我心中唤起了与福楼拜相同的愿望——「哦，但愿我身在贝都因人中间！」

8 月 7 日，传来大祸的消息。皇帝匆匆离开圣克卢，赶赴战场。敌人已打进国境。报纸对「入侵」的怒火怎样发泄都嫌不够炽烈。在我看来，「打到柏林去」（À Berlin）的呐喊所指向的正是蓄意的入侵；而这并没有什么可愤怒的。可这些东方野蛮人竟敢进犯美丽、蒙上帝垂爱的法兰西——那才是十足的残暴与罪孽。必须制止，而且要快。

临时陆军部长颁布法令：凡三十至四十岁、有服役能力而不属国民自卫军之列的公民，应立即编入该军。新设了一个国防部门。业经表决的战争公债由 5 亿法郎（500 million）追加为 10 亿法郎（1000 million）。看着人们总是何等慷慨地献上别人的金钱与别人的生命，实在令人心旷神怡。

===Original===

A trifling financial unpleasantness, to be sure, was soon perceptible to the public. If one wanted to change bank notes one had to pay the money-changer ten percent. There was not gold at hand to meet all the notes which the Bank of France was authorised to issue.
And now, victory after victory on the German side.
The physiognomy of the city of Paris and its inhabitants altered. Instead of its proud, magnificent, resplendent mood, came confusion and savage indignation. The feeling spread ever wider and wider that a horde of Vandals had descended on to the land﻿—something terrible, unheard of, like some cloud of locusts, or some such natural portent. That they had themselves brought this plague on themselves by their declaration of war﻿—that they had considered such a declaration indispensable, in order that no Hohenzollern, even in the distant future, should even conceive the idea of succeeding to the Spanish throne﻿—all that they had forgotten. Hideous tales were circulated about the enemy. “The Uhlans! the Uhlans!” These words had a fantastically-demoniacal sound, as if one had said “the horde of savages.” In the imagination of the people this kind of troops assumed a demoniacal shape. Wherever a bold stroke was executed by the German cavalry, it was attributed to the Uhlans﻿—a kind of half-men, getting no pay, and therefore bound to live on their plunder. Along with the rumours of terror arose rumours also of triumph. To tell lies about successes is one of the duties of Chauvinism. Of course, because courage must be kept up. The command, to tell truth, like so many other commands, loses its obligation in war time. Frederick dictated to me the following passage out of the newspaper *Le Volontaire* for my red book:﻿—

当然，一桩小小的金融上的不快，很快便让公众察觉了。想兑换银行券，得付给兑换商一成佣金。法兰西银行获准发行的银行券，手头已没有足够的黄金来应付。

而这时，德军一边一场接一场的胜利。

巴黎城与巴黎人的面目变了。先前那种骄傲、豪迈、光彩照人的心绪不见了，代之以惶惑与狂暴的义愤。一种感觉愈传愈广：一帮汪达尔人杀进了国土——某种可怕骇人的东西，像一大片蝗群，或诸如此类的天降凶兆。至于这场瘟疫正是他们自己宣战招到头上来的——至于他们曾认定这一宣战必不可少，为的是叫任何霍亨索伦家的人哪怕在遥远的将来也起不了继承西班牙王位的念头——这一切他们全忘了。关于敌人的种种可怖传闻四下流传。「乌兰骑兵！乌兰骑兵！」这几个字带着一种离奇魔鬼般的声响，就像有人说「野蛮人部落」一样。在这种部队身上，民众的想象力给它安上了魔怪的形象。德军骑兵无论在哪里出击得手，都被记在乌兰骑兵头上——一种半人半魔的家伙，领军饷是没有的，因此只好靠掳掠过活。与恐怖的谣言一同兴起的还有胜利的谣言。谎报战功乃是沙文主义的义务之一。当然啦，因为总得叫人保持勇气嘛。「不可说谎」这条诫命，同许多别的诫命一样，一到战时便失去了约束力。弗雷德里克从《志愿兵报》（Le Volontaire）上给我口述了下面一段，记进我的红皮日记本（red book）：——

===Original===

> Up to the 16th of August, the Germans have lost already 144,000 men. The rest are almost starving. The last reserves are coming up from Germany﻿—“*la landwehr et la landsturm.*” Old men of sixty, with flint muskets, with an enormous tobacco pouch on their right side and a still larger schnaps-flask on their left, a long clay pipe in their mouth; stooping under the weight of the knapsack (on the top of which there must not be omitted the coffee mill and the elder tea inside), are crawling along, coughing and blowing their noses, from the right to the left bank of the Rhine, cursing those who have torn them from the embraces of their grandchildren, to lead them on to certain death. “As to the news of victory, brought from German sources,” it was said in the French newspapers, “they are the usual Prussian lies.”

> 截至 8 月 16 日，德军已折损 144,000 人。其余的差不多都在挨饿。最后的预备队正从德国开来——「后备军与国民军（la landwehr et la landsturm）」。60 岁的老人，扛着燧发枪，右边挂着一只硕大无朋的烟叶袋，左边挂着一只更大的烧酒瓶，嘴里叼着长长的陶土烟斗；被背包的重量压弯了腰（背包顶上那台咖啡磨和里头装着的接骨木茶是断不可遗漏的），一边咳嗽一边擤着鼻涕，从莱茵河右岸爬向左岸，咒骂着那些把他们从孙儿怀抱里拽出来、驱向必死之地的人。「至于德国方面传来的捷报，」法国报纸上说，「都是普鲁士人惯常的谎话。」

On August 20 Count Palikao announced in the Chamber that three army corps which had coalesced against Bazaine had been thrown into the quarries at Jaumont (Bravo! Bravo!). It is true that no one knew what quarries these were, or where they were; nor did anyone explain how they could contain three army corps; but the joyous message went round from mouth to mouth. “Have you heard? In the quarries﻿—” “Oh yes! Of Jaumont.” No one uttered a doubt or question. It was as if everybody had been born at Jaumont, and knew these army-swallowing quarries as well as his own pocket. About this time the rumour also prevailed that the King of Prussia had *gone mad* from despair at the condition of his army.
Nothing but monstrous things were heard of. The excitement, the fever, of the populace increased hourly. The war “*là-bas*” had ceased to be regarded as an armed promenade. It was felt that the forces which had been let loose were now bringing something terrible on the world. Nothing was spoken of but armies annihilated, princes driven mad, diabolical hordes, war to the knife. I listened to it thundering and growling. It was the storm of rage and despair that was rising. The battle at Bazeilles near Metz was described, and it was stated that inhuman cruelties had been committed there by the Bavarians.
“Do you believe that?” I asked Frederick. “Do you believe that of the gentle Bavarians?”
“It is quite possible. Bavarian or Turco, German, French, or Indian, the warrior who is defending his own life, and lifting up his arm to kill another, has ceased for the time to be ‘human.’ What has been awakened in him and stirred up with all possible force is nothing else than bestiality.”
---
Metz fallen! The news resounded in the city like some strange and overpowering cry of terror. To me the news of the taking of a fortress was a message which brought rather a relief; for I thought, “Well, that is decisive.” And it was only for this, that the bloody game might be over, it was for this, only this that I longed. But no, there was nothing decisive in it﻿—more fortresses remained. After a defeat all that is to be done is to pick yourself up again, and strike out again at them twice as hard. The chance of arms may change at any time. Ah yes! The advantage may be now on this side, now on that. It is only woe that is certain﻿—death that is certain﻿—to be on both.

===Chinese===

8 月 20 日，帕利科伯爵在议院宣布：合力对付巴赞的三个军已被掷进雅蒙的采石场（好哇！好哇！）。诚然，谁也不知道那是些什么采石场、在哪儿；也没人解释它们怎么装得下三个军；但这喜讯却口口相传。「听说了吗？扔进采石场了——」「哦，是啊！雅蒙的。」没有一个人说出怀疑或疑问。仿佛人人都是在雅蒙出生的，对那几张吞军的采石场熟悉得就像自己的口袋。大约与此同时，还盛行着一个谣言：普鲁士国王因自己军队的处境而绝望，疯了。

听到的净是些骇人听闻的事。民众的激动与狂热与时俱增。那边（là-bas）的战争不再被当作一场武装郊游了。人们感到，被放出来的那些力量如今正把某种可怕的东西带到世上。人们嘴上谈的尽是全歼的军团、逼疯的君王、魔鬼般的游群、你死我活的血战。我听着这一切轰轰隆隆、咕咕作响。那是愤怒与绝望的风暴正在升起。人们描绘梅斯近郊巴泽耶的战斗，说巴伐利亚人在那里犯下了惨绝人寰的暴行。

「你信吗？」我问弗雷德里克。「你说性情温和的巴伐利亚人会干出这种事，你信吗？」

「很有可能。巴伐利亚人也好，土尔克兵也好，德国人、法国人、印度人也好，一个为保自己性命而举起手臂去杀人的战士，此刻已不复是『人』了。在他身上被唤醒、并被竭尽全力煽动起来的，不是别的，正是兽性。」

---

梅斯陷落了！这消息在全城回荡，像一声奇异而势不可当的惊呼。在我听来，一座要塞陷落的消息反倒带来几分宽慰；因为我想：「好啊，这下总算见分晓了。」我渴盼的只是这个——只盼这场血腥的赌局就此收场，我盼的就是这个，只是这个。可是不，这里面没有任何决定性的东西——还有的是要塞呢。吃了一场败仗，要做的无非是重新爬起来，再加倍狠地打回去。武运随时可能改变。是啊！优势也许今天在这边，明天在那边。只有苦难是确定无疑的——死亡是确定无疑的——对两边都是。
